# How to use this guide

Industrial Pharmacy I is a descriptive subject: most marks come from well-organised lists, flow charts and tables of excipients, methods, defects and tests. Study one unit a day. Read the notes, then close them and write out each flow chart (wet granulation, sugar coating, capsule shell making, parenteral production, lyophilisation, aerosol filling) from memory. Finish with the question bank and the MCQs for that unit.

The notes follow the five units of the PCI syllabus exactly. Unit 2 is the largest (tablets plus liquid orals) and is split into Part A and Part B inside one file; Unit 4 (parenterals and ophthalmics) and Unit 5 (cosmetics, aerosols and packaging) are also in parts. No unit has been merged or moved.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

The question bank has long (10-mark), short (5-mark) and very short (2-mark) questions. The very short ones are good warm-ups and help with MCQs.

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; prepare the full answer with a flow chart or table.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from common patterns and syllabus weight, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Preformulation | Goals of preformulation, polymorphism, flow properties (angle of repose, Carr's index), solubility and partition coefficient, hydrolysis and oxidation, BCS |
| 2 Tablets and liquid orals | Granulation methods, tablet excipients, processing problems (capping, picking), coating types and defects, IP tests (weight variation, friability, disintegration, dissolution), syrups, suspensions and emulsions |
| 3 Capsules and pellets | Hard shell manufacture, capsule sizes and filling machines, soft gelatin capsules (rotary die, base adsorption, minim/gram factor), capsule QC, pelletisation |
| 4 Parenterals and ophthalmics | Types and requirements of parenterals, vehicles and additives, production area and clean rooms, lyophilisation, containers, QC tests (sterility, pyrogen, LAL, particulate, leaker), eye drops and ointments |
| 5 Cosmetics, aerosols, packaging | Lipstick, shampoo, cold and vanishing creams, toothpaste, hair dyes, sunscreens; aerosol components, propellants, filling and evaluation; packaging materials, interactions and glass tests |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. Open every answer with a one-line definition, then go to a numbered list; examiners in this subject reward structure.
2. Draw a flow chart for any process (granulation, coating, shell manufacture, rotary die, parenteral production, lyophilisation, pelletisation, aerosol filling). A neat chart can carry half the marks.
3. Use tables for excipients (class, purpose, examples) and for defects (defect, cause, remedy). Give two examples for every class.
4. Learn the official numbers exactly: IP weight variation for tablets (10, 7.5, 5%) and capsules (10, 7.5%), friability (100 revolutions, not more than 1%), disintegration times (15, 30, 60, 3, 5 minutes; enteric 2 h in acid), autoclave 121 °C for 15 minutes, 0.9% NaCl isotonic, sterility test media and temperatures, particulate limits for LVPs.
5. For a "write a note on" question, finish with uses or significance; for a "formulation" question, give a typical ingredient list with the role of each.
6. Compare-type questions (wet vs dry granulation, sugar vs film coating, hard vs soft capsules, flocculated vs deflocculated, cold vs vanishing cream, cold vs pressure filling) are best answered as a table.
7. Practise the small calculations: Carr's index and Hausner ratio, capsule size from fill weight and density, friability %, tonicity adjustment, base adsorption and minim/gram factor.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you only have an hour, prepare these with a flow chart or table each: **granulation methods**, **tablet processing problems and coating defects**, **IP quality control tests of tablets**, **hard and soft gelatin capsule manufacture**, **parenteral production area and QC tests**, and **aerosol propellants and filling**. Together they cover most 10-mark questions.

**Unit 1 — Preformulation**

- Goals: profile the drug, spot problems, choose salt and form, guide dosage form and process.
- Amorphous: faster dissolving, less stable. Stable polymorph: highest melting point, lowest solubility. Detect by XRD, DSC, TGA, hot-stage microscopy, IR.
- Flow: tan θ = h/r; Carr's index = 100(ρt − ρb)/ρt; Hausner = ρt/ρb. Good flow: θ 31–35°, CI 11–15%, HR 1.12–1.18.
- Weak acid S = S0[1 + 10^(pH − pKa)]; log P by octanol–water shake flask.
- Degradation: hydrolysis (aspirin, procaine, penicillins), oxidation (adrenaline, ascorbic acid, oils), racemisation (hyoscyamine → atropine), polymerisation (ampicillin).
- BCS I high/high; II low sol; III low perm; IV both low. High solubility: highest dose in ≤250 ml, pH 1–6.8.

**Unit 2 — Tablets and liquid orals**

| Item | Key facts |
| --- | --- |
| Excipients | Diluent, binder, disintegrant, glidant, lubricant, antiadherent, colour, flavour, sweetener |
| Granulation | Wet (mix → wet mass → screen → dry → size → lubricate); dry (slugging, roller compaction); direct compression |
| Problems | Capping/lamination (air, fines, dryness), picking/sticking (moisture, low lubricant), chipping, mottling, double impression |
| Sugar coating | Seal → subcoat → smooth → colour → polish → print |
| Film coat | Polymer (HPMC) + plasticiser (PEG) + solvent + colour; enteric: CAP, HPMCP, Eudragit L/S |
| Coating defects | Blistering, chipping, cratering, picking, pitting, blooming, blushing, orange peel, cracking, twinning, infilling |
| IP weight variation | ≤80 mg 10%; 80–250 mg 7.5%; ≥250 mg 5% (20 tablets) |
| Friability | 25 rpm × 4 min = 100 revolutions; loss ≤1% |
| Disintegration | Uncoated 15, film 30, sugar 60, dispersible 3, effervescent 5 min; enteric 2 h acid then buffer pH 6.8 |
| Dissolution | Basket/paddle, 900 ml, 37 °C; S1 6 units ≥ Q + 5% |
| Liquids | Simple Syrup IP ≈ 66.7% w/w; Stokes' law; F = Vu/Vo; dry gum 4:2:1 |

**Unit 3 — Capsules and pellets**

- Gelatin A (acid, pork, IEP 7–9), B (alkali, bone, IEP 4.7–5). Hard shell moisture 13–16%.
- Shell making: dip → spin → dry → strip → trim → join.
- Sizes: 000 1.37, 00 0.95, 0 0.68, 1 0.50, 2 0.37, 3 0.30, 4 0.21, 5 0.13 ml.
- Filling: hand plate, auger, dosator, dosing disc. Capsule weight variation: <300 mg 10%; ≥300 mg 7.5%.
- Soft capsule: gelatin + glycerin/sorbitol + water; rotary die (Scherer); BA = g base/g solid; M/g = minims of solid + its base per g.
- Pellets 0.5–1.5 mm: extrusion–spheronisation (MCC), layering, spray drying/congealing, cryopelletisation.

**Unit 4 — Parenterals and ophthalmics**

- Sterile, pyrogen-free, particle-free, stable, isotonic (0.9% NaCl, −0.52 °C).
- WFI by distillation; oily vehicles IM only; no preservative in LVP (≥100 ml).
- Production: wash → depyrogenate (dry heat ~250 °C) → compound → filter (0.22 µm) → fill → seal → sterilise (121 °C, 15 min) → test → pack.
- Clean rooms: Grade A (ISO 5, laminar flow), B, C, D; HEPA ≥ 99.97% at 0.3 µm.
- Lyophilisation: freeze → primary drying (sublimation) → secondary drying.
- Glass Type I borosilicate, II treated soda-lime, III soda-lime. Pull sealing of ampoules.
- QC: sterility (FTM 30–35 °C, SCDM 20–25 °C, 14 days), BET (LAL), rabbit pyrogen, particulate (LVP ≤25/ml ≥10 µm, ≤3/ml ≥25 µm), leaker test (methylene blue).
- Eye: sterile, preserved (benzalkonium chloride + edetate), viscosity agents; ointment base soft paraffin + liquid paraffin + wool fat; metal particle test.

**Unit 5 — Cosmetics, aerosols, packaging**

| Product | Core formula |
| --- | --- |
| Lipstick | Beeswax, carnauba, castor oil, lanolin, eosin/pigments, perfume |
| Shampoo | SLS/SLES, betaine, conditioner, NaCl, preservative |
| Cold cream (w/o) | Beeswax, liquid paraffin, borax, water |
| Vanishing cream (o/w) | Stearic acid, KOH/TEA, glycerin, water |
| Toothpaste | Abrasive, humectant, binder, SLS, saccharin, flavour, fluoride |
| Hair dye (permanent) | p-Phenylenediamine + coupler + H2O2 + ammonia |
| Sunscreen | Chemical (PABA, cinnamates, benzophenones, avobenzone) and physical (ZnO, TiO2); SPF = MED ratio |

- Aerosol parts: concentrate, propellant, container, valve, actuator. Propellants: CFC (banned), HFA-134a/227ea, hydrocarbons, compressed gases. Systems: two-phase, three-phase, suspension, foam, barrier. Filling: cold, pressure, compressed gas. Tests: flame projection, vapour pressure, spray pattern, dose uniformity, particle size, hot water bath leak test.
- Packaging: primary/secondary/tertiary; glass, plastics, metals, rubber, paper. Interactions: permeation, leaching, sorption, chemical reaction, modification. Container terms: well-closed, tightly closed, hermetic, light-resistant, tamper-evident.

# Preformulation studies on paracetamol (or aspirin)

**Aim:** To carry out preformulation studies on paracetamol (or aspirin or any other drug given by your teacher): organoleptic properties, melting point, solubility, bulk and tapped density, flow properties (angle of repose, Carr's index, Hausner ratio) and loss on drying.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles and a lab coat. All numbers in the worked examples below are specimen readings for practice, not standard values.

## Principle

Preformulation describes the physical and chemical nature of a drug before it is formulated. Flow properties decide whether a powder can be compressed directly or must be granulated. Density gives an idea of packing and compressibility. Solubility and melting point help identify the drug and predict its behaviour.

- Angle of repose: tan θ = h/r
- Carr's index (%) = 100 × (ρt − ρb)/ρt
- Hausner ratio = ρt/ρb

## Requirements

Drug powder (paracetamol IP), funnel with stand, graph paper, 100 ml measuring cylinder, tapped density apparatus (or tapping by hand from a fixed height), balance, melting point apparatus with capillary tubes, test tubes, solvents (water, ethanol, chloroform, ether, 0.1 M HCl, 0.1 M NaOH), hot-air oven, weighing bottle, desiccator.

## Procedure

**A. Organoleptic properties**

1. Note colour, odour, taste (only if the teacher allows) and appearance under a hand lens.

**B. Melting point**

2. Fill a capillary to about 3 mm with dry powder, place in the melting point apparatus and heat slowly near the expected range. Record the temperature range from first melting to complete melting.

**C. Solubility**

3. Add about 10 mg of drug to 1 ml of each solvent, shake, and add solvent in portions until it dissolves. Express the result using the pharmacopoeial descriptive terms.

**D. Bulk and tapped density**

4. Weigh about 25 g (W) of powder, pour gently through a funnel into a 100 ml cylinder and read the bulk volume (Vb).
5. Tap the cylinder (mechanically or by hand from a fixed height) until the volume does not change; read tapped volume (Vt).

**E. Angle of repose (fixed funnel method)**

6. Fix a funnel so its tip is 2 cm above graph paper. Pour powder until the heap just touches the tip.
7. Mark the base circle, measure the diameter at several points and find the radius r; h is the height of the heap.

**F. Loss on drying**

8. Weigh about 1 g in a dried, weighed bottle; dry at 105 °C (or as per the monograph) to constant weight; cool in a desiccator and weigh.

## Observations and calculations

| Test | Reading | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Colour, odour | | |
| Melting range (°C) | | |
| Weight W (g) | | |
| Bulk volume Vb (ml) | | ρb = W/Vb |
| Tapped volume Vt (ml) | | ρt = W/Vt |
| Height h (cm), radius r (cm) | | θ = tan⁻¹(h/r) |
| Loss on drying (%) | | |

**Worked example (specimen readings).** W = 25 g, Vb = 62.5 ml, Vt = 50 ml. ρb = 0.40 g/ml; ρt = 0.50 g/ml. Carr's index = 100 × (0.50 − 0.40)/0.50 = **20%** (fair). Hausner ratio = 0.50/0.40 = **1.25** (fair). Heap h = 2.0 cm, r = 2.6 cm → tan θ = 0.77, θ ≈ **37.6°** (fair).

**Interpretation:** a powder with fair or poorer flow is usually wet-granulated before compression. Paracetamol crystals flow and compress poorly, which is why it is normally granulated.

Loss on drying (%) = 100 × (weight before − weight after)/weight before.

## Result

The drug was ________ in appearance, melted at ______ °C, was ________ (descriptive term) in water, had bulk density ____ g/ml, tapped density ____ g/ml, Carr's index ____%, Hausner ratio ____ and angle of repose ____°, indicating ______ flow.

## Precautions

1. Pour powder gently for bulk volume; do not shake or press it.
2. Keep the funnel height fixed and avoid vibration while forming the heap.
3. Heat slowly (about 1–2 °C per minute) near the melting point.
4. Use dry powder and dry glassware.

## Viva questions

1. **What is preformulation?** Study of drug properties before formulation to design a stable, effective dosage form.
2. **What does a high Carr's index mean?** A more compressible, more cohesive powder with poorer flow.
3. **How can flow be improved?** Granulation, adding a glidant (colloidal silica), larger or more spherical particles, drying.
4. **Why does paracetamol need granulation?** It flows and compresses poorly (tablets cap easily).
5. **What is the difference between bulk and tapped density?** Bulk includes air spaces of loose packing; tapped is after the powder settles by tapping.
6. **Name two instrumental methods for polymorphs.** X-ray powder diffraction and differential scanning calorimetry.

# Preparation and evaluation of paracetamol tablets

**Aim:** To prepare and submit paracetamol tablets (500 mg) by wet granulation and to evaluate them.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles and a lab coat.

## Principle

Paracetamol crystals flow poorly and do not bind well on compression, so tablets made by direct compression often cap. Wet granulation with starch paste gives free-flowing, compressible granules. Starch also acts as a disintegrant; magnesium stearate and talc lubricate and help flow.

## Formula (typical, for 100 tablets of about 600 mg)

| Ingredient | Per tablet | For 100 tablets | Role |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Paracetamol | 500 mg | 50.0 g | Drug |
| Starch (as 10% paste) | about 25 mg | about 2.5 g | Binder |
| Starch (dry, disintegrant) | about 40 mg | about 4.0 g | Disintegrant |
| Lactose or microcrystalline cellulose | to adjust | q.s. | Diluent |
| Talc | about 1% | about 0.6 g | Glidant/antiadherent |
| Magnesium stearate | about 0.5–1% | about 0.3–0.6 g | Lubricant |

## Requirements

Mortar and pestle or planetary mixer, sieves (about 10/12 and 16/22 mesh), tray dryer or hot-air oven, single punch or rotary tablet press with 12–13 mm punches, balance, beakers, water bath; for evaluation: vernier calliper, hardness tester, friabilator, disintegration test apparatus, dissolution apparatus, UV spectrophotometer.

## Procedure

1. Pass paracetamol, half of the dry starch and the diluent through a sieve and mix well.
2. Prepare starch paste: disperse starch in a little cold water, add hot water with stirring and heat until translucent; cool.
3. Add paste gradually to the powder with mixing until a damp mass forms that holds together when squeezed and breaks cleanly (ball test).
4. Pass the wet mass through a 10/12 mesh sieve.
5. Dry the granules at about 50–60 °C until moisture is low (check loss on drying, about 1–2%).
6. Pass the dried granules through a 16/22 mesh sieve.
7. Add the remaining starch (extragranular), talc and finally magnesium stearate; blend gently for a few minutes only (over-mixing the lubricant slows disintegration).
8. Evaluate the granules (bulk density, Carr's index, angle of repose).
9. Compress on the tablet press, adjusting fill weight and hardness.
10. Evaluate the tablets as below and pack in a well-closed container.

## Evaluation and observations

| Test | Method | Specimen reading |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Appearance | Visual | White, round, smooth |
| Thickness/diameter | Vernier calliper (10 tablets) | e.g. 4.8 mm / 12.7 mm |
| Uniformity of weight | 20 tablets weighed singly | see example |
| Hardness | Monsanto or similar (5 tablets) | e.g. 5–6 kg |
| Friability | 100 revolutions | see example |
| Disintegration | IP apparatus, water 37 °C | e.g. 6 min |
| Dissolution / assay | As per monograph, UV | |

**Worked example: uniformity of weight (specimen data).** Total of 20 tablets = 12.10 g → average 605 mg. Since average is ≥250 mg, the allowed deviation is 5% → range 574.8–635.3 mg; twice the limit (10%) → 544.5–665.5 mg. If no more than 2 tablets lie outside 574.8–635.3 mg and none outside 544.5–665.5 mg, the batch passes.

**Worked example: friability (specimen data).** 11 tablets (6.65 g) before; 6.62 g after 100 revolutions. Friability = 100 × (6.65 − 6.62)/6.65 = **0.45%** → passes (not more than 1%).

## Result

Paracetamol tablets were prepared by wet granulation and evaluated. Average weight ____ mg; hardness ____ kg; friability ____%; disintegration time ____ min. The tablets complied / did not comply with IP limits.

## Precautions

1. Do not over-wet the mass; it gives hard granules and slow disintegration.
2. Dry granules at moderate temperature to the right moisture; too dry granules cap.
3. Add magnesium stearate last and mix briefly.
4. Clean punches and dies before and after compression.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is paracetamol wet-granulated?** Poor flow and compressibility; it tends to cap.
2. **Role of starch paste?** Binder; dry starch acts as disintegrant.
3. **Why add part of the disintegrant after granulation?** Extragranular disintegrant breaks the tablet into granules quickly.
4. **What causes capping?** Trapped air, fines, too-dry granules, worn tooling, high speed.
5. **IP disintegration limit for uncoated tablets?** 15 minutes.
6. **Why is hardness not an official test?** It depends on tablet size and type; it is an in-process control.

# Preparation and evaluation of aspirin tablets

**Aim:** To prepare aspirin tablets (300 or 325 mg) and evaluate them, including a limit check for free salicylic acid.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles and a lab coat.

## Principle

Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) hydrolyses in the presence of moisture and heat to salicylic acid and acetic acid (vinegar odour). Wet granulation with water is therefore avoided; tablets are made by **dry granulation (slugging)** or direct compression, or by non-aqueous granulation. Alkaline lubricants such as magnesium stearate speed hydrolysis, so **talc** or stearic acid is preferred. Starch acts as disintegrant.

## Formula (typical, per tablet)

| Ingredient | Quantity | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Aspirin (crystalline) | 300 mg | Drug |
| Starch (dried) | about 30–40 mg | Disintegrant/diluent |
| Talc | about 10–15 mg | Lubricant/glidant |
| (Optional) microcrystalline cellulose | q.s. | Dry binder, aids compression |

## Requirements

Dried starch, sieves, heavy tablet press with flat punches for slugging, regular punches for final tablets, balance, evaluation equipment (as for paracetamol), ferric chloride solution, test tubes.

## Procedure (slugging method)

1. Dry the starch at about 105 °C and cool in a desiccator.
2. Mix aspirin with half the starch (and MCC if used) and part of the talc.
3. Compress into large, flat slugs on the press at high pressure.
4. Break the slugs in a mortar and pass through a 12/16 mesh sieve to get granules.
5. Add the remaining starch and talc; blend gently.
6. Compress into tablets of the calculated weight.
7. Evaluate and pack in a tightly closed container with desiccant, protected from moisture.

## Evaluation

As for any uncoated tablet: appearance, weight variation, thickness, hardness, friability, disintegration (15 minutes), and dissolution/assay. Also:

**Test for free salicylic acid (limit check by colour):** shake powdered tablets with water and filter; add dilute ferric chloride. Salicylic acid gives a violet colour; compare with a standard containing the permitted amount (as in the monograph). An intense violet colour shows hydrolysis.

**Worked example: uniformity of weight (specimen data).** 20 tablets weigh 7.00 g → average 350 mg (≥250 mg → 5% limit). Range 332.5–367.5 mg; twice the limit 315–385 mg. Readings: one tablet at 330 mg, all others within range → passes.

## Result

Aspirin tablets were prepared by slugging using talc as lubricant. Average weight ____ mg; hardness ____ kg; friability ____%; disintegration ____ min; free salicylic acid test ______.

## Precautions

1. Keep everything dry; work quickly in low humidity.
2. Do not use magnesium stearate or other alkaline excipients.
3. Do not heat aspirin.
4. Store in a tightly closed container with desiccant.

## Viva questions

1. **Why not wet-granulate aspirin with water?** It hydrolyses in moisture and heat.
2. **Why is magnesium stearate avoided?** Its alkalinity catalyses hydrolysis.
3. **What does a vinegar smell from aspirin tablets mean?** Hydrolysis has released acetic acid.
4. **What is slugging?** Dry granulation: large tablets (slugs) are compressed and broken into granules.
5. **Test for salicylic acid?** Violet colour with ferric chloride.
6. **Other ways to make aspirin tablets?** Direct compression; roller compaction; non-aqueous granulation.

# Film coating of tablets or granules

**Aim:** To film-coat the given tablets (or granules) with a hydroxypropyl methylcellulose (HPMC) film and to evaluate the coated product.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles and a lab coat. Use organic solvents only in a well-ventilated area away from flames.

## Principle

A thin polymer film is sprayed onto tablets rotating in a coating pan while warm air evaporates the solvent. The film masks taste, protects from moisture and light, and improves appearance. A coating solution contains a film-forming polymer, a plasticiser, a solvent and a colourant/opacifier.

## Formula of coating solution (typical, about 100 ml)

| Ingredient | Quantity | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HPMC (low viscosity grade) | about 4–6 g | Film former |
| Polyethylene glycol 400 or 6000 | about 0.5–1 g | Plasticiser |
| Titanium dioxide | about 0.5 g | Opacifier |
| Colour (lake or iron oxide) | q.s. | Colour |
| Purified water (or ethanol–water) | to 100 ml | Solvent |

(For an enteric coat, the teacher may use cellulose acetate phthalate in acetone–ethanol with diethyl phthalate as plasticiser.)

## Requirements

Laboratory coating pan with hot-air blower, spray gun with compressor (or atomiser), core tablets (pre-dusted), beakers, stirrer, sieve, balance, disintegration apparatus.

## Procedure

1. Disperse HPMC in part of hot water, then add the rest as cold water with stirring until clear; add PEG.
2. Disperse titanium dioxide and colour in a little of the solution (homogenise or grind) and add to the bulk; pass through a fine sieve.
3. Weigh 20 core tablets (W1) and record their appearance.
4. Load de-dusted tablets into the pan; warm them with hot air while rotating slowly.
5. Spray the coating solution in short bursts, allowing each layer to dry before the next; adjust pan speed, spray rate and air temperature to avoid sticking or roughness.
6. Continue until the required weight gain (commonly about 2–4%) is reached.
7. Dry the coated tablets in the pan for some minutes with warm air, then cool.
8. Weigh 20 coated tablets (W2) and evaluate.

## Observations and calculations

% weight gain = 100 × (W2 − W1)/W1

**Worked example (specimen readings).** 20 cores = 6.000 g; 20 coated = 6.180 g. Weight gain = 100 × 0.180/6.000 = **3.0%**.

| Test | Uncoated | Coated |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Appearance | | |
| Average weight (mg) | | |
| Thickness (mm) | | |
| Disintegration (min) | | (IP limit for film-coated: 30 min) |
| Defects seen | | |

## Result

The tablets were film-coated with HPMC; weight gain ____%; appearance ______; disintegration time ____ min.

## Precautions

1. De-dust core tablets first.
2. Do not over-wet the bed: spray slowly and let each layer dry, or tablets will stick (picking, twinning).
3. Do not over-heat (blistering, blushing).
4. Keep the spray gun clean and the solution stirred.

## Viva questions

1. **Role of plasticiser?** Makes the film flexible and prevents cracking.
2. **Name two film formers.** HPMC and ethylcellulose (also methacrylate copolymers).
3. **What is orange peel?** Rough coat from a viscous solution drying before it spreads.
4. **Enteric coating polymers?** CAP, HPMCP, Eudragit L/S, shellac.
5. **Advantages of film over sugar coating?** Faster, thinner, little weight gain, keeps logos visible.
6. **IP disintegration time for film-coated tablets?** 30 minutes.

# Preparation and evaluation of tetracycline capsules

**Aim:** To prepare and submit tetracycline hydrochloride capsules (250 mg) in hard gelatin capsules and evaluate them.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear gloves, goggles and a lab coat; tetracycline is an antibiotic powder, so avoid inhaling dust.

## Principle

The drug is blended with a diluent, glidant and lubricant to give a free-flowing powder, which is filled into hard gelatin capsules of a size chosen from the fill weight and the tapped density of the blend. Calcium-containing diluents (dicalcium phosphate, calcium carbonate) are **not** used because tetracycline forms chelates with calcium and is then poorly absorbed; lactose or starch is used instead.

## Formula (typical, per capsule)

| Ingredient | Quantity | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tetracycline hydrochloride | 250 mg | Drug |
| Lactose (or starch) | q.s. to fill weight | Diluent |
| Colloidal silicon dioxide or talc | about 0.5–1% | Glidant |
| Magnesium stearate | about 0.5–1% | Lubricant |

## Requirements

Mortar and pestle or blender, sieve (about 60–80 mesh), balance, empty hard gelatin capsules (size 1 or 0), hand-operated capsule filling machine (or tile and spatula), measuring cylinder for tapped density, disintegration apparatus with discs.

## Procedure

1. Determine the tapped density of the drug–diluent blend (see calculation).
2. Choose the capsule size and calculate the diluent needed to fill it.
3. Sift drug and diluent; mix by geometric dilution; add glidant and finally lubricant; mix briefly.
4. Place empty capsules in the filling machine, separate caps, spread the powder evenly over the bodies and level it; tamp lightly; repeat until filled.
5. Replace caps and lock; remove filled capsules.
6. Clean the outside by rolling in a cloth (or tumbling with salt crystals) to remove adhering powder.
7. Evaluate and pack in a well-closed, light-resistant container.

## Calculations

Fill volume needed = fill weight ÷ tapped density.

**Worked example (specimen readings).** Drug blend tapped density = 0.75 g/ml. A size 1 capsule holds about 0.50 ml → can hold 0.50 × 0.75 = 0.375 g = **375 mg**. Drug 250 mg + lubricant/glidant about 4 mg → diluent ≈ 375 − 254 = **121 mg** per capsule. For 50 capsules plus 10% excess for losses (55 capsules): drug 13.75 g, lactose 6.66 g, magnesium stearate and glidant about 0.11 g each.

## Evaluation

| Test | Method | Specimen reading |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Appearance | Colour, locking, no dents or powder outside | |
| Uniformity of weight | 20 capsules: weigh intact, empty, weigh shells, find contents | see example |
| Disintegration | IP apparatus with discs, water 37 °C | e.g. 8 min (usual limit 30 min) |
| Assay / dissolution | As per monograph | |

**Worked example: uniformity of weight (specimen data).** Average content weight = 372 mg (≥300 mg → 7.5% limit). Range 344.1–399.9 mg; twice the limit (15%) 316.2–427.8 mg. If not more than two contents fall outside the first range and none outside the second, the batch passes.

## Result

Tetracycline hydrochloride capsules (250 mg) were prepared in size ___ capsules. Average content ____ mg; uniformity of weight ______; disintegration time ____ min.

## Precautions

1. Do not use calcium salts as diluent.
2. Protect from light and moisture (tetracycline degrades to toxic epi- and anhydro- products).
3. Fill uniformly; level the powder before closing.
4. Handle shells with dry, gloved hands.

## Viva questions

1. **Why not dicalcium phosphate as diluent?** Calcium chelates tetracycline and reduces absorption.
2. **How is capsule size chosen?** From fill weight and tapped density of the blend.
3. **Volume of size 0 and 1 capsules?** About 0.68 ml and 0.50 ml.
4. **IP weight variation for capsules?** 10% if less than 300 mg, 7.5% if 300 mg or more.
5. **Why should tetracycline be protected from light and moisture?** Degradation products are less active and can be toxic.
6. **Name automatic capsule filling principles.** Auger, dosator, dosing disc (tamping).

# Preparation of calcium gluconate injection

**Aim:** To prepare and submit calcium gluconate injection (10% w/v) in ampoules.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, gloves and a lab coat. Work in the cleanest area available and handle hot ampoules and flames with care.

## Principle

Calcium gluconate is used in calcium deficiency (hypocalcaemia, tetany). Its solubility in cold water is low, so a 10% w/v solution is supersaturated and tends to crystallise on standing. A small quantity of a more soluble calcium salt, usually calcium D-saccharate, is included as a stabiliser (within the proportion allowed by the monograph). The solution is made with Water for Injections, filtered, filled into ampoules, sealed and sterilised by autoclaving.

## Formula (typical)

| Ingredient | Quantity for 100 ml | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Calcium gluconate | 10 g | Drug |
| Calcium D-saccharate | small quantity as permitted | Stabiliser (prevents crystallisation) |
| Water for Injections | to 100 ml | Vehicle |

## Requirements

Calcium gluconate IP, stabiliser, Water for Injections, beakers, glass rod, hot plate, sintered glass filter or membrane filter assembly, 10 ml ampoules (cleaned and dry-heat sterilised), syringe or burette for filling, gas–oxygen burner for sealing, autoclave, methylene blue solution for leaker test, black and white inspection boards.

## Procedure

1. Clean ampoules: wash with water and detergent, rinse with purified water and then WFI, dry and sterilise by dry heat.
2. Heat about 80 ml of WFI nearly to boiling; dissolve the stabiliser and then calcium gluconate with stirring.
3. Make up to 100 ml with hot WFI.
4. Filter while hot through a sintered glass or membrane filter to get a clear solution.
5. Fill 10 ml (plus a small overfill) into each ampoule using a syringe with a long needle, keeping the neck dry.
6. Seal by pull sealing (or tip sealing) in the flame.
7. Sterilise in the autoclave at 121 °C for 15 minutes.
8. Carry out the leaker test, clarity test and label.

## Calculations

**Worked example (batch calculation).** Required: 10 ampoules × 10 ml. Add overfill and loss allowance (say 10 ampoules × 10.5 ml = 105 ml, plus about 15% for filter and transfer losses ≈ 120 ml). Calcium gluconate needed = 10 g per 100 ml × 120 ml = **12 g** in 120 ml of solution.

## Evaluation

| Test | Observation |
| --- | --- |
| Clarity (against black and white backgrounds) | Clear, no visible particles |
| Leaker test (methylene blue under vacuum) | No dye entered |
| Fill volume (extractable volume) | |
| pH (as in the monograph) | |

## Result

Calcium gluconate injection 10% w/v was prepared, filled into ___ ampoules of 10 ml each, sterilised by autoclaving and found clear and free from leakers.

## Label

Calcium Gluconate Injection IP, 10% w/v, 10 ml; for intravenous use (slow injection); batch number; date of preparation; storage: do not refrigerate (crystallisation); discard if crystals are seen.

## Precautions

1. Use freshly prepared WFI and sterile, pyrogen-free glassware.
2. Dissolve with heat; filter hot to avoid crystallisation.
3. Do not wet the ampoule neck while filling (charring on sealing).
4. Inspect every ampoule for particles after sterilisation.

## Viva questions

1. **Use of calcium gluconate injection?** Hypocalcaemia, tetany, some cases of hyperkalaemia and magnesium toxicity.
2. **Why is a stabiliser added?** A 10% solution is supersaturated and may crystallise.
3. **Why should it not be refrigerated?** Low temperature encourages crystallisation.
4. **Method of sterilisation?** Autoclaving at 121 °C for 15 minutes.
5. **What is pull sealing?** Neck heated while rotating and the top pulled away, giving a strong seal.
6. **What is the leaker test?** Ampoules immersed in dye under vacuum; leaking ones take up dye.

# Preparation of ascorbic acid injection

**Aim:** To prepare and submit ascorbic acid injection (for example 500 mg in 5 ml, i.e. 10% w/v) in ampoules.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, gloves and a lab coat.

## Principle

Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) is strongly acidic in solution, which is painful on injection, so part of it is converted into sodium ascorbate with sodium bicarbonate to raise the pH. Carbon dioxide is released in this reaction. Ascorbic acid oxidises easily, especially in the presence of air and metal ions, so the solution is prepared with WFI freed from dissolved oxygen, a chelating agent (disodium edetate) and sometimes an antioxidant are added, and the ampoules are flushed and filled under nitrogen. The solution is sterilised as directed; filtration through a 0.22 µm membrane with aseptic filling is the gentler method for this oxidation-prone drug.

## Formula (typical, for 100 ml)

| Ingredient | Quantity | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ascorbic acid | 10 g | Drug |
| Sodium bicarbonate | enough to bring pH to the monograph range (several grams) | pH adjustment (forms sodium ascorbate) |
| Disodium edetate | small quantity (e.g. about 0.01–0.05 g) | Chelating agent |
| Water for Injections (boiled, cooled under nitrogen) | to 100 ml | Vehicle |
| Nitrogen gas | q.s. | Displaces oxygen |

## Requirements

Ascorbic acid IP, sodium bicarbonate, disodium edetate, WFI, nitrogen cylinder with sterile filter on the line, pH meter, membrane filtration assembly (0.22 µm), sterile ampoules, burner, laminar airflow bench if available, amber ampoules or light-protective cartons.

## Procedure

1. Boil WFI and cool it while bubbling nitrogen through it.
2. Dissolve disodium edetate and ascorbic acid in about 80 ml of this water under a nitrogen stream.
3. Add sodium bicarbonate slowly in small portions with gentle stirring, letting the CO2 escape (avoid frothing over).
4. Check pH and adjust within the range in the monograph; make up to 100 ml with nitrogen-saturated WFI.
5. Filter through a sterile 0.22 µm membrane into a sterile receiver.
6. Flush sterile ampoules with nitrogen, fill aseptically (5 ml + overfill), flush the headspace with nitrogen and seal at once.
7. Leaker test, clarity check, label and store protected from light.

## Calculations

**Worked example (stoichiometry, illustrative).** Ascorbic acid (C6H8O6, Mr 176.12) reacts with NaHCO3 (Mr 84.01) 1 : 1. To neutralise 1.0 g of ascorbic acid completely would need 84.01/176.12 = 0.477 g NaHCO3. Because only part of the acid is neutralised to reach the target pH, the amount used is found by titrating with a pH meter, not by full calculation.

**Batch:** 10 ampoules × 5 ml with 0.25 ml overfill = 52.5 ml; with about 15% loss allowance, prepare 60 ml → ascorbic acid 6.0 g.

## Result

Ascorbic acid injection (10% w/v) was prepared under nitrogen, sterilised by filtration, filled into ___ ampoules of 5 ml and found clear and colourless.

## Precautions

1. Keep oxygen out at every step (nitrogen-saturated water, nitrogen flushing).
2. Use metal-free equipment where possible; add edetate to bind metal ions.
3. Add bicarbonate slowly because of effervescence.
4. Protect from light; discard yellow or brown solutions (oxidation).

## Viva questions

1. **Why is sodium bicarbonate added?** To raise pH and reduce pain by forming sodium ascorbate.
2. **Why is nitrogen used?** To displace oxygen and prevent oxidation.
3. **Role of disodium edetate?** Chelates metal ions that catalyse oxidation.
4. **Sign of degradation?** Yellow to brown colour.
5. **Why filtration rather than heat?** Heat speeds oxidation of ascorbic acid.
6. **Pore size of sterilising filter?** 0.22 µm.

# Quality control tests of marketed tablets and capsules (as per IP)

**Aim:** To perform IP quality control tests on a marketed brand of tablets and of capsules and to report whether they comply.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles and a lab coat. The worked results below are specimen readings for practice.

## Principle

Official tests check that every unit contains the right amount of drug and will release it in the body: uniformity of weight, friability, disintegration and dissolution (with hardness and dimensions as useful non-official checks).

## Requirements

Marketed tablets (e.g. a 500 mg brand) and capsules, analytical balance, vernier calliper, hardness tester, Roche friabilator, IP disintegration apparatus (with discs), dissolution apparatus (basket/paddle), UV spectrophotometer, media.

## Procedure

**Tablets**

1. **Appearance:** note shape, colour, markings, defects.
2. **Thickness and diameter:** measure 10 tablets with a vernier calliper.
3. **Uniformity of weight:** weigh 20 tablets individually; find the average and the % deviation of each.
4. **Hardness:** test 5–10 tablets; note mean and range.
5. **Friability:** take tablets weighing about 6.5 g (if each weighs 650 mg or less; else 10 tablets), de-dust, weigh, rotate 100 times (25 rpm, 4 min), de-dust, reweigh.
6. **Disintegration:** 6 tablets in the basket-rack, water at 37 ± 2 °C; note the time for all to disintegrate (uncoated 15 min, film-coated 30 min, sugar-coated 60 min).
7. **Dissolution:** as per the monograph (apparatus, medium, rpm, time); measure absorbance and calculate % released.

**Capsules**

8. **Uniformity of weight:** weigh an intact capsule, open it, empty fully (wipe shell), weigh the shell; content = intact − shell. Repeat for 20 capsules.
9. **Disintegration:** 6 capsules with discs, water at 37 °C; hard capsules usually within 30 minutes.

## Observations and calculations

**Uniformity of weight of tablets (specimen data; average 0.6200 g).** Limit for ≥250 mg is 5% → 0.5890–0.6510 g; twice the limit 0.5580–0.6820 g.

| No. | Weight (g) | % deviation | No. | Weight (g) | % deviation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.6210 | +0.16 | 11 | 0.6180 | −0.32 |
| 2 | 0.6150 | −0.81 | 12 | 0.6260 | +0.97 |
| 3 | 0.6330 | +2.10 | 13 | 0.6200 | 0.00 |
| 4 | 0.6050 | −2.42 | 14 | 0.6170 | −0.48 |
| … | … | … | … | … | … |

% deviation = 100 × (individual − average)/average. In this example all lie within ±5% → **complies**.

**Friability (specimen):** 6.512 g before; 6.487 g after → 100 × 0.025/6.512 = **0.38%** → complies.

**Capsule content weight (specimen):** average content 255 mg (<300 mg → 10% limit) → range 229.5–280.5 mg; none outside → **complies**.

**Dissolution (specimen):** absorbance of test 0.452, standard (equivalent to 100% release) 0.470 → % released = 100 × 0.452/0.470 = **96.2%**.

## Result

| Test | Tablets | Capsules | Complies? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Uniformity of weight | | | |
| Friability | | — | |
| Hardness (kg) | | — | — |
| Disintegration (min) | | | |
| Dissolution (%) | | | |

## Precautions

1. Use a calibrated balance; handle units with forceps.
2. De-dust tablets before and after friability.
3. Maintain medium temperature at 37 °C.
4. Empty capsules completely without damaging shells.

## Viva questions

1. **IP weight variation for tablets of 80 mg or less?** 10%.
2. **Why is hardness non-official?** It depends on size, shape and purpose of the tablet.
3. **What is Q in dissolution?** Amount of drug (as % of label) that must dissolve in the stated time.
4. **Why are discs used in disintegration?** To keep units submerged and add gentle mechanical action.
5. **What if a friability test shows broken tablets?** The batch fails regardless of % loss.
6. **Content uniformity is needed for which products?** Low-dose units where weight does not reflect drug content.

# Preparation of eye drops and eye ointment

**Aim:** To prepare and submit (a) chloramphenicol eye drops 0.5% w/v and (b) chloramphenicol eye ointment 1% w/w (or other preparations given by your teacher).

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, gloves and a lab coat. Work aseptically, ideally under a laminar airflow bench.

## Principle

Eye preparations must be sterile, free of irritating particles, close to isotonic and at a tolerable pH. Multi-dose drops contain a preservative. Chloramphenicol loses activity on prolonged heating, so the drops are sterilised by filtration and filled aseptically. The eye ointment base (soft paraffin, liquid paraffin and wool fat) is sterilised by dry heat and the drug is incorporated aseptically.

## Formulae (typical)

**(a) Chloramphenicol eye drops**

| Ingredient | Quantity for 100 ml | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chloramphenicol | 0.5 g | Drug |
| Boric acid | about 1.5 g | Buffer, tonicity |
| Borax | about 0.3 g | Buffer |
| Phenylmercuric nitrate | about 0.002 g | Preservative |
| Purified water (sterile) | to 100 ml | Vehicle |

**(b) Chloramphenicol eye ointment**

| Ingredient | Quantity for 100 g | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chloramphenicol (very fine powder) | 1 g | Drug |
| Liquid paraffin | about 10 g | Softens base, levigating agent |
| Wool fat | about 10 g | Emollient, takes up water |
| Yellow soft paraffin | to 100 g | Base |

## Requirements

Ingredients, beakers, water bath, 0.22 µm membrane filter assembly, sterile dropper bottles, hot-air oven, sterile ointment slab and spatula (or mortar), sterile eye-ointment tubes, laminar airflow bench.

## Procedure

**(a) Eye drops**

1. Dissolve boric acid, borax and phenylmercuric nitrate in about 90 ml of hot purified water; cool to about 60 °C.
2. Add chloramphenicol and stir until dissolved; cool and make up to volume.
3. Filter through a sterile 0.22 µm membrane into a sterile receiver.
4. Fill aseptically (for example 10 ml) into sterile dropper bottles; close at once.

**(b) Eye ointment**

5. Melt the wool fat, liquid paraffin and soft paraffin together; filter hot through coarse filter paper or muslin.
6. Sterilise the base by dry heat (for example 160 °C for 2 hours) in a covered container.
7. Levigate the sterile, very finely powdered chloramphenicol with a little sterile liquid paraffin or base on a sterile slab, then add the remaining cooled base by geometric dilution.
8. Fill into sterile eye-ointment tubes aseptically; close and crimp.

## Calculations

**Tonicity check (worked example with specimen values).** Suppose the sodium chloride equivalents are boric acid E = 0.50 and chloramphenicol E = 0.10 (use the values in your reference table).
NaCl-equivalent of 100 ml = (1.5 × 0.50) + (0.5 × 0.10) + (borax contribution, ignored here) ≈ 0.80 g → about 0.8% NaCl equivalent, which is close to isotonic (0.9%) and well tolerated by the eye.

**Ointment for 20 tubes of 4 g with 10% excess:** 88 g total → chloramphenicol 0.88 g, liquid paraffin 8.8 g, wool fat 8.8 g, yellow soft paraffin 69.5 g.

## Evaluation

Clarity of drops (black and white backgrounds); pH; sterility (if facilities allow); fill volume; for the ointment, homogeneity and absence of gritty particles, leakage of tubes, metal particles test (IP).

## Result

Chloramphenicol eye drops 0.5% w/v (___ bottles) and chloramphenicol eye ointment 1% w/w (___ tubes) were prepared aseptically.

## Labels

Eye drops: "Sterile. For external use only. Do not use more than 4 weeks after first opening. Store in a refrigerator if stated by the monograph. Protect from light." Eye ointment: "Sterile eye ointment. For external use only."

## Precautions

1. Work aseptically with sterile containers and tools.
2. Do not heat chloramphenicol drops for long (loss of potency).
3. Use very finely powdered drug in the ointment to avoid eye irritation.
4. Close containers immediately after filling.

## Viva questions

1. **Why must eye preparations be sterile?** The eye has weak defences; infection (e.g. Pseudomonas) can cause loss of sight.
2. **Role of boric acid–borax?** Buffer and tonicity adjustment.
3. **Why add a viscosity agent to some drops?** To prolong contact time with the eye.
4. **Why wool fat in eye ointment base?** It is emollient and helps take up water from tears.
5. **How is the ointment base sterilised?** By dry heat.
6. **Common preservative in eye drops?** Benzalkonium chloride (here phenylmercuric nitrate).
practicals.title: Preparation of eye drops and eye ointment

# Preparation of cold cream and vanishing cream

**Aim:** To prepare and submit (a) a cold cream (beeswax–borax type) and (b) a vanishing cream (stearic acid type), and to compare them.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles and a lab coat. Potassium hydroxide is corrosive.

## Principle

**Cold cream** is mainly a water-in-oil emulsion. Borax reacts with the free fatty acids of beeswax to form a sodium soap in situ, which emulsifies the water in the oil phase. Evaporation of water gives a cooling effect.

**Vanishing cream** is an oil-in-water emulsion. Part of the stearic acid is saponified by an alkali (potassium hydroxide or triethanolamine) to form stearate soap, which emulsifies the remaining stearic acid. It spreads to an invisible, non-greasy film.

## Formulae (typical, for 100 g)

**(a) Cold cream**

| Ingredient | Quantity | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| White beeswax | about 16 g | Emulsifier source, stiffener |
| Liquid paraffin | about 50 g | Oil phase, emollient |
| Borax | about 1 g | Forms soap with beeswax acids |
| Purified water | to 100 g | Aqueous phase |
| Perfume, preservative | q.s. | |

**(b) Vanishing cream**

| Ingredient | Quantity | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stearic acid | about 18 g | Main oil phase, forms soap |
| Potassium hydroxide | about 0.8–1 g (or triethanolamine about 1–2 g) | Saponifies part of stearic acid |
| Glycerin | about 8 g | Humectant |
| Purified water | to 100 g | Aqueous phase |
| Perfume, preservative (e.g. methyl paraben) | q.s. | |

## Requirements

Beakers, water bath, thermometer, glass rod or mechanical stirrer, balance, porcelain dish, ointment jars.

## Procedure

**(a) Cold cream**

1. Melt beeswax and liquid paraffin together on a water bath at about 70–75 °C.
2. Dissolve borax (and preservative) in water and heat to the same temperature.
3. Add the aqueous phase slowly to the oil phase with continuous stirring.
4. Stir while the cream cools; add perfume at about 40 °C; continue stirring till it sets.
5. Fill into a jar.

**(b) Vanishing cream**

6. Melt stearic acid at about 75 °C.
7. Dissolve potassium hydroxide (or triethanolamine), glycerin and preservative in water; heat to 75 °C.
8. Add the aqueous phase to the melted stearic acid with constant stirring in one direction.
9. Keep stirring as it cools; a white, smooth cream with a pearly sheen forms; add perfume at about 40 °C.
10. Fill into a jar.

## Calculations

**Scaling (worked example).** To make 30 g of vanishing cream from the 100 g formula, multiply each quantity by 0.3: stearic acid 5.4 g, KOH 0.27 g, glycerin 2.4 g, water to 30 g.

**Emulsion type tests**

| Test | Cold cream | Vanishing cream |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dilution with water | Does not mix (w/o) | Mixes (o/w) |
| Water-soluble dye (amaranth) | Scattered coloured droplets | Uniform colour |
| Conductivity | Poor | Conducts |

## Evaluation

Appearance, colour, odour, texture, pH, spreadability, type of emulsion, washability, phase separation on standing or centrifuging.

## Result

Cold cream (w/o) and vanishing cream (o/w) were prepared and the emulsion type of each confirmed.

## Precautions

1. Both phases must be at the same temperature before mixing.
2. Add phases slowly with steady stirring; avoid beating in air.
3. Add perfume after cooling to about 40 °C to prevent loss.
4. Handle KOH with care.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is cold cream cooling?** Water evaporates from the skin.
2. **What emulsifies cold cream?** Sodium soap formed from borax and beeswax fatty acids.
3. **Why is vanishing cream non-greasy?** It is o/w and leaves a thin stearic acid film.
4. **Role of glycerin?** Humectant.
5. **What gives the pearly sheen?** Crystals of stearic acid.
6. **How to test emulsion type?** Dilution, dye and conductivity tests.

practicals.markdown:
# Evaluation of glass containers (as per IP)

**Aim:** To evaluate the given glass containers by tests of the Indian Pharmacopoeia: hydrolytic resistance (powdered glass test and water attack test) and related checks, and to identify the type of glass.

> Quantities and procedure details are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and the current IP for exact quantities, strengths of titrant and limits. Wear goggles, gloves and a lab coat; crushed glass is sharp.

## Principle

Glass in contact with water releases alkali (mainly sodium), which raises pH and can degrade drugs. The amount of alkali released under standard autoclaving conditions is measured by titration with dilute acid using methyl red, and the result is compared with IP limits to decide the glass type:

- **Powdered glass test** — on crushed glass of a fixed size; tests the bulk glass; used to tell Type I from Type III.
- **Water attack test** — on whole containers filled with water; tests the treated inner surface; used for Type II.

## Requirements

Containers to be tested, mortar and pestle (hardened steel) or glass crusher, sieves (as specified in the IP), acetone, magnet (to remove iron from crushing), conical flasks of resistant glass, autoclave, burette, standard dilute acid (strength as in IP), methyl red solution, purified water (carbon dioxide-free), balance.

## Procedure

**A. Powdered glass test**

1. Rinse and dry the containers; crush pieces in the mortar and sieve to collect the size fraction specified in the IP.
2. Wash the grains with acetone to remove fine dust; dry; remove iron particles with a magnet.
3. Weigh the specified amount (for example 10 g) into a flask, add the specified volume of purified water, cover and autoclave at 121 °C for the specified time.
4. Cool, decant the water, wash the grains and titrate the combined liquid with the standard acid using methyl red.
5. Do a blank titration with water alone and subtract.

**B. Water attack test (for Type II)**

6. Rinse containers with purified water; fill to about 90% of capacity with CO2-free purified water.
7. Cover and autoclave at 121 °C for the specified time; cool.
8. Pool the contents, take a measured volume and titrate with the standard acid using methyl red; subtract a blank.

**C. Other checks (where facilities allow)**

9. Visual inspection for cracks, bubbles, stones and uneven wall thickness.
10. Light transmission test for amber (light-resistant) glass using a spectrophotometer.
11. Arsenic limit test for glass meant for aqueous parenteral preparations.
12. Thermal shock test (sudden transfer between hot and cold water) and check for annealing with a polariscope.

## Observations and calculations

| Sample | Weight or volume taken | Burette reading (test, ml) | Blank (ml) | Net volume (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Powdered glass | | | | |
| Water attack | | | | |

Net volume = test − blank. Express the result as ml of the standard acid for the quantity specified in the IP and compare with the IP table of limits for each glass type.

**Worked example (specimen readings only).** Powdered glass test: test titre 0.30 ml, blank 0.05 ml → net 0.25 ml for the specified 10 g. A low value like this falls in the range expected for highly resistant (Type I) glass; a much larger value would point to soda-lime (Type III) glass. Always check the actual limit in the IP edition you use.

## Result

The given glass containers released ____ ml of standard acid in the powdered glass test (and ____ ml in the water attack test) and are classified as Type ____ glass.

## Precautions

1. Remove fine dust with acetone so that results reflect true surface attack.
2. Use CO2-free water and resistant-glass flasks for the test.
3. Carry out a blank under identical conditions.
4. Handle crushed glass and hot autoclaved flasks carefully.

## Viva questions

1. **What does the powdered glass test measure?** Alkali released from the bulk of crushed glass under autoclaving.
2. **Which test is used for Type II glass and why?** Water attack test, because its resistance lies in the treated surface, which crushing would destroy.
3. **Composition of Type I glass?** Borosilicate glass.
4. **Why is amber glass used?** It cuts off light that degrades drugs.
5. **Why is the arsenic test done?** Arsenic compounds are used in glass making and could leach into injections.
6. **Indicator used in the titration?** Methyl red.
