# Unit 2: Tablets and liquid orals

Tablets are the most widely used dosage form in India and worldwide, and this is the heaviest unit of the subject. The first part covers how tablets are formulated, made, coated and tested; the second part covers the manufacture and evaluation of syrups, elixirs, suspensions and emulsions.

## Part A: Tablets

## 2.1 Introduction and ideal characteristics

A **tablet** is a solid unit dosage form containing one or more drugs, with or without excipients, made by compressing (or occasionally moulding) a powder or granules into a fixed shape.

**Advantages:** accurate dose in each unit; cheap to make in large numbers; easy to carry, swallow, pack and identify; better chemical stability than liquids; taste can be masked by coating; can be designed for delayed or sustained release.

**Disadvantages:** hard for children, elderly and unconscious patients to swallow; poorly compressible or poorly wettable drugs are difficult to formulate; slow onset compared with injections; some drugs irritate the gut.

**Ideal characteristics of a tablet**

1. Elegant appearance, free of cracks, chips, specks and contamination.
2. Enough strength to survive packing and transport, yet able to disintegrate and dissolve when swallowed.
3. Correct and uniform weight and drug content.
4. Releases the drug in a predictable, reproducible way (bioavailable).
5. Chemically and physically stable through its shelf life.
6. Acceptable to the patient in size, shape, taste and odour.

## 2.2 Classification of tablets

| Group | Types |
| --- | --- |
| Oral, swallowed | Compressed (plain), multiple compressed (layered, compression-coated), sugar-coated, film-coated, enteric-coated, chewable, controlled/sustained release |
| Used in the mouth | Buccal, sublingual (glyceryl trinitrate), lozenges and troches, dental cones, mouth-dissolving (orally disintegrating) |
| Taken after dissolving or dispersing | Effervescent, dispersible, soluble tablets |
| Other routes | Vaginal tablets, implants, hypodermic tablets (obsolete) |

## 2.3 Excipients used in tablets

| Class | Purpose | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Diluents (fillers) | Give bulk to make a tablet of practical size | Lactose, microcrystalline cellulose, dibasic calcium phosphate, starch, mannitol (chewable tablets), sucrose |
| Binders | Hold particles together in granules and tablets | Starch paste (about 5–10%), gelatin, acacia, polyvinylpyrrolidone (povidone), HPMC, methylcellulose, sucrose solution |
| Disintegrants | Break the tablet apart in fluid | Starch (about 5–10%), microcrystalline cellulose; superdisintegrants at low levels: croscarmellose sodium, sodium starch glycolate, crospovidone |
| Glidants | Improve flow of granules into the die | Colloidal silicon dioxide, talc |
| Lubricants | Reduce friction between tablet and die wall; help ejection | Magnesium stearate (commonly around 0.25–1%), stearic acid, talc, PEG, sodium stearyl fumarate |
| Antiadherents | Stop sticking to punch faces | Talc, colloidal silica, corn starch |
| Others | Appearance, taste, absorption, stability | Colours (lakes), flavours, sweeteners (saccharin, aspartame), wetting agents (sodium lauryl sulphate), adsorbents, buffers |

**How disintegrants work:** swelling (sodium starch glycolate), wicking or capillary action (microcrystalline cellulose, crospovidone), deformation recovery, and gas release (effervescent couple).

**Methods of adding disintegrant:** intragranular (inside the granules), extragranular (mixed with dry granules before compression) or both; adding part on each side gives fastest break-up into fine particles.

## 2.4 Granulation methods

**Why granulate?** To improve flow, improve compressibility, prevent segregation of ingredients, give uniform content, reduce dust, and control density.

### a. Wet granulation

```text
Weigh and sift drug + diluent (+ part of disintegrant)
   → dry mix
   → add binder solution → wet massing (dough-like mass)
   → wet screening (about 6–12 mesh)
   → drying (tray dryer or fluidised bed dryer)
   → dry screening (about 14–20 mesh)
   → add lubricant, glidant, extragranular disintegrant → final blend
   → compression
```

- **Equipment:** planetary mixer, sigma-blade mixer, high-shear mixer granulator (mixes, wets and granulates in one bowl), fluidised bed granulator (spray binder onto a fluidised powder; mixes, granulates and dries in one unit), oscillating granulator and multimill for sizing.
- **Advantages:** good flow and compressibility; uniform content of low-dose drugs; hydrophobic drugs become more wettable.
- **Disadvantages:** many steps, time, space and energy; not for moisture- or heat-sensitive drugs.
- **End point of wet massing:** the "ball test" (mass squeezed in the hand forms a ball that breaks cleanly), or power consumption of the mixer.

### b. Dry granulation

Used for moisture- or heat-sensitive drugs (aspirin, some vitamins) and when the drug compresses well.

- **Slugging:** large flat tablets ("slugs") are made on a heavy-duty press, then broken and sieved into granules.
- **Roller compaction:** powder is squeezed between two counter-rotating rollers into a sheet (ribbon), which is milled into granules. More controllable and faster than slugging.

### c. Direct compression

The drug is simply blended with directly compressible excipients and compressed. Needs excipients with good flow and compressibility: spray-dried lactose, microcrystalline cellulose, dibasic calcium phosphate dihydrate, directly compressible starch, mannitol.

- **Advantages:** fewest steps, cheapest, no heat or water, faster disintegration into primary particles.
- **Limits:** high-dose drugs with poor flow cannot be made this way; risk of segregation; special excipients cost more.

## 2.5 Compression: machines and tooling

**Steps in compression:** die filling → weight adjustment (excess removed) → compression between upper and lower punches → ejection by the lower punch → tablet pushed off the die table.

| Machine | Features | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single punch (eccentric) press | One die and one pair of punches; upper punch does the compressing; noisy, intermittent | Small, for research and small batches |
| Rotary (multi-station) press | Many dies on a rotating turret; both punches move; compression between rollers; feed frame fills dies | Very high, used in industry |
| Double rotary / high-speed press | Two compression points per turn; induced (force) feeders | Even higher |

**Tablet tooling:** the set of **upper punch, lower punch and die**. Punch parts: head, barrel, stem, tip (face). Tooling standards are named B and D type (D type is larger for bigger tablets); the IPT (Indian), TSM and EU standards describe dimensions. Punch face shapes: flat-faced, flat bevel-edged, shallow, standard and deep concave, and shaped (oval, capsule). Embossing and break lines are made on punch faces. Tooling must be polished, inspected for wear and stored oiled.

**Parts of a rotary press:** hopper, feed frame, die table (turret), upper and lower punches, cams (raise and lower punches), weight-adjustment cam, pre-compression and main compression rollers, ejection cam, take-off blade.

## 2.6 Processing problems in tablet manufacture

| Problem | What you see | Main causes | Remedies |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Capping | Top or bottom cap separates | Air trapped in granules, too many fines, too dry granules, worn or deep-concave tooling, too fast compression | Pre-compression, slower speed, more binder, right moisture, remove fines, new tooling |
| Lamination | Tablet splits into layers | Same as capping; also too much lubricant | As for capping |
| Picking | Material removed from tablet surface by punch face, esp. in embossing | Moist granules, too little lubricant, sharp embossing | Dry granules, more antiadherent, better embossing design, chromium-plated punches |
| Sticking | Granules stick to punch faces or die wall | Excess moisture, low-melting ingredients, little lubricant | Dry well, more lubricant, cool room |
| Chipping | Edges break off | Damaged punches, brittle granules | Polish/replace tooling, adjust binder |
| Cracking | Fine cracks on top surface | Fast expansion, deep-concave punches | Tapered dies, adjust formula |
| Mottling | Uneven colour | Dye migration during drying, colour differences of drug and excipient | Change solvent, use lakes, mill finer |
| Double impression | Embossing appears twice | Free-rotating lower punch that turns after first impression | Anti-turning device on punches |
| Binding | Tablet hard to eject, scored sides | Too little lubricant, moist granules, rough die | More lubricant, dry, polish dies |
| Weight variation | Uneven weights | Poor flow, wide granule size range, uneven die filling, segregation | Glidant, uniform granules, induced feeder |
| Hardness variation | Uneven strength | Weight variation, punch length differences | Correct fill, uniform tooling |

## 2.7 Tablet coating

**Reasons for coating:** mask bitter taste or smell; protect from moisture, light and air; protect the stomach from the drug or the drug from stomach acid (enteric coating); control release; improve appearance and identification; make swallowing easier.

### Types of coating

1. **Sugar coating** — traditional, thick, elegant, but slow and heavy.
2. **Film coating** — thin polymer film; fast and light; most common today.
3. **Enteric coating** — resists stomach acid and dissolves in the intestine.
4. **Compression (press) coating** — a coat compressed around a core in a special press.
5. **Controlled-release coating** — insoluble polymer membranes (ethylcellulose, methacrylate copolymers).

### Sugar coating steps

```text
Core tablets (de-dusted)
 1 Sealing     → water-proof layer (shellac, CAP, zein) to keep water out of the core
 2 Subcoating  → rounds edges and builds up the tablet (sugar syrup + gum + fillers such as talc, CaCO3)
 3 Smoothing   → thin syrup coats fill irregularities (grossing)
 4 Colouring   → syrup with soluble dye or insoluble pigment (lakes)
 5 Polishing   → waxes (beeswax, carnauba) in a canvas-lined pan
 6 Printing    → edible ink for identification
```

A sugar coat may double the tablet weight; the process takes hours to days and needs skilled operators.

### Film coating: formulation of coating composition

| Component | Role | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Film-forming polymer | Forms the film | HPMC, hydroxypropyl cellulose, methylcellulose, ethylcellulose (insoluble, for release control), povidone, polyvinyl alcohol, methacrylate copolymers |
| Plasticiser | Makes the film flexible, lowers glass transition | Polyethylene glycol, propylene glycol, glycerin, triethyl citrate, diethyl phthalate, castor oil |
| Solvent | Carries the polymer | Water (preferred now), ethanol, isopropanol, acetone, methylene chloride (organic solvents are being replaced) |
| Colourant / opacifier | Colour, light protection | Iron oxides, lakes, titanium dioxide |
| Others | Flavour, surfactant, antitacking agent | Talc, polysorbates |

**Enteric coating materials:** cellulose acetate phthalate (CAP), hydroxypropyl methylcellulose phthalate (HPMCP), polyvinyl acetate phthalate, methacrylic acid copolymers (Eudragit L and S types), shellac. They carry acidic groups that stay un-ionised in the stomach and ionise and dissolve at intestinal pH.

**Uses of enteric coating:** drugs destroyed by acid (erythromycin, pancreatin, omeprazole), drugs that irritate the stomach (aspirin, NSAIDs), drugs meant for local action in the intestine.

### Methods and equipment for coating

| Equipment | How it works | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Standard (conventional) coating pan | Inclined rotating pan, coating solution ladled or sprayed, hot air blown on surface | Simple; poor drying for film coating |
| Pan with immersion tube or immersion sword | Sprays and dries through a tube/sword in the tablet bed | Better drying |
| Perforated pans (e.g. Accela-Cota, Hi-Coater, Glatt type) | Side-vented or fully perforated drum; air passes through the bed | Efficient, automated; used for film coating |
| Fluidised bed (air-suspension, Wurster) coater | Tablets or pellets suspended in an air stream; spray from bottom through a partition column | Good for small particles and pellets |
| Compression coater | Press coats a core with dry granules | No solvent |
| Electrostatic and dip coating | Charge or dipping | Specialised |

Spray guns may be airless (high pressure) or air-spray (atomised by compressed air).

### Defects in coating

| Defect | Description | Cause and remedy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Blistering | Film detaches as bubbles | Too high drying temperature traps vapour; dry more gently |
| Chipping | Film chips off at edges | Brittle film or pan too fast; more plasticiser, gentler pan |
| Cratering | Volcano-like craters exposing the core | Coating liquid penetrates core; control spray rate and drying |
| Picking | Pieces of film torn away | Tablets stick together while wet; reduce spray rate, raise drying |
| Pitting | Small pits on surface | Core temperature above melting point of an ingredient |
| Blooming | Film goes dull after storage | Low-molecular-weight plasticiser migrates; change plasticiser or level |
| Blushing | Whitish specks or haze | Polymer precipitates from too-hot drying; lower temperature |
| Colour variation | Uneven colour | Poor mixing, uneven spray, migration of soluble dye |
| Infilling | Break line or logo filled in | Foam or droplets in the logo; less foam, better atomisation |
| Orange peel (roughness) | Bumpy, orange-skin surface | Coating liquid too viscous or dries too fast before spreading |
| Cracking | Film cracks | Internal stress; use more plasticiser or higher-molecular-weight polymer |
| Twinning | Two tablets stuck together | Flat-faced tablets, slow drying; change shape, faster drying |

## 2.8 Quality control tests for tablets

### In-process quality control (IPQC)

Checked at intervals during compression: average weight and weight variation, thickness, hardness, friability, disintegration and appearance. During granulation: moisture content (loss on drying), granule size distribution, bulk density, flow and blend uniformity.

### Finished product tests

1. **General appearance:** size, shape, colour, odour, taste, surface texture, markings.
2. **Thickness and diameter:** measured with a vernier calliper or micrometer; must stay within a narrow range for packing and for uniform appearance.
3. **Uniformity of weight (IP):** weigh 20 tablets individually and find the average. Not more than two tablets may differ from the average by more than the percentage below, and none by more than twice that percentage.

| Average weight of tablet | Allowed deviation |
| --- | --- |
| 80 mg or less | 10% |
| More than 80 mg and less than 250 mg | 7.5% |
| 250 mg or more | 5% |

4. **Hardness (crushing strength):** force needed to break a tablet diametrically. Testers: Monsanto, Pfizer, Strong-Cobb, Erweka and modern motorised testers. Not an official test; a value around 4 kg is commonly quoted as the minimum for a satisfactory conventional tablet (chewable and orally disintegrating tablets are softer, sustained-release ones harder).
5. **Friability:** Roche friabilator turns at 25 rpm for 4 minutes (100 revolutions), dropping the tablets about 6 inches each turn. For tablets of unit weight 650 mg or less, take whole tablets weighing as near as possible to 6.5 g; for heavier tablets take 10 tablets. De-dust, weigh, rotate, de-dust and reweigh. % friability = 100 × (initial − final)/initial; a loss of not more than 1% is generally acceptable, with no broken tablets.
6. **Disintegration test (IP):** basket-rack assembly with six tubes and a 10-mesh screen, raised and lowered in water (or the stated medium) at 37 ± 2 °C. Usual IP times unless the monograph says otherwise:

| Tablet type | Time |
| --- | --- |
| Uncoated | 15 minutes |
| Film-coated | 30 minutes |
| Sugar-coated | 60 minutes |
| Dispersible | 3 minutes |
| Effervescent | 5 minutes |
| Enteric-coated | No disintegration in 0.1 M HCl for 2 hours; then disintegrates in phosphate buffer pH 6.8 within 60 minutes |

7. **Dissolution test:** measures the rate at which drug goes into solution. IP Apparatus 1 (basket) and Apparatus 2 (paddle); 900 ml medium at 37 ± 0.5 °C. Acceptance by stages: S1 six units, each not less than Q + 5%; S2 six more, average of 12 not less than Q and none less than Q − 15%; S3 twelve more, average of 24 not less than Q, not more than two below Q − 15% and none below Q − 25% (Q = amount stated in the monograph).
8. **Uniformity of content:** for low-dose tablets the drug is assayed in 10 single tablets. In the classic IP test each should lie within 85–115% of the average; if one lies outside this but within 75–125%, 20 more are tested. Newer editions also give the harmonised "uniformity of dosage units" test based on an acceptance value; follow the edition your college uses.
9. **Assay:** drug content of a powdered pooled sample, within the monograph limits.
10. Others where needed: moisture, microbial limits, wetting/coating tests, uniformity of dispersion (dispersible tablets).

## Part B: Liquid orals

## 2.9 Syrups and elixirs

**Syrup:** a concentrated, viscous aqueous solution of sucrose or another sugar, with or without flavours and medicaments. **Simple Syrup IP** is about 66.7% w/w sucrose in purified water; at this strength it resists microbial growth because so little free water is available (high osmotic pressure).

**Components:** sugar (sucrose; sorbitol or glycerin in sugar-free syrups), purified water, preservatives (methyl and propyl paraben, sodium benzoate), flavours, colours, the drug, sometimes alcohol, buffers and antioxidants.

**Manufacture:** (1) solution with heat — sugar dissolved in heated water (overheating causes inversion to glucose and fructose and caramelisation, darkening); (2) agitation without heat for heat-sensitive ingredients; (3) adding sucrose to a medicated liquid; (4) percolation (water passed slowly through a bed of sucrose). Syrup is filtered, made up to volume and filled hot or cold.

**Problems:** crystallisation of sugar (cap locking) if too concentrated; fermentation if too dilute; inversion and colour change if overheated.

**Elixir:** a clear, sweetened, hydroalcoholic solution for oral use. Alcohol helps dissolve drugs that are poorly soluble in water and acts as a preservative; glycerin, propylene glycol and sorbitol are also used. Examples: paracetamol and antihistamine elixirs. Prepared by simple solution; the alcoholic and aqueous parts are mixed with care because adding water can precipitate oils (filter with talc to clarify).

## 2.10 Suspensions

A **suspension** is a coarse dispersion of insoluble solid particles in a liquid (usually aqueous) vehicle. Used for insoluble drugs, to mask taste (insoluble salt), and for drugs unstable in solution.

**Ideal suspension:** settles slowly; sediment redisperses easily on gentle shaking; does not cake; pours easily; uniform dose per spoonful; pleasant taste.

**Stokes' law:** v = d²(ρs − ρl)g / 18η. Settling slows when particle size d is small, the density difference small and viscosity η high.

**Flocculated vs deflocculated**

| Property | Flocculated | Deflocculated |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Particles | Loose aggregates (flocs) | Separate particles |
| Settling | Fast | Slow |
| Sediment | Loose, high volume, easy to redisperse | Compact; forms a hard cake |
| Supernatant | Clear quickly | Stays cloudy |
| Approach | Controlled flocculation with electrolytes, surfactants or polymers | Needs a structured vehicle to prevent caking |

**Formulation components:** wetting agents (polysorbates, glycerin, alcohol) for hydrophobic powders; suspending/viscosity agents (acacia, tragacanth, sodium alginate, methylcellulose, sodium CMC, xanthan gum, bentonite, Veegum); flocculating agents (electrolytes, surfactants); preservatives; buffers; sweeteners, flavours, colours.

**Manufacture:** mill drug to fine size → wet with wetting agent → disperse suspending agent in vehicle (hydrated) → mix drug slurry with vehicle → add other ingredients → make up volume → homogenise (colloid mill) → fill with continuous stirring so each bottle gets the same content. Many antibiotics are supplied as dry powder for reconstitution.

**Evaluation of suspensions:**

- **Sedimentation volume F = Vu/Vo** (ultimate sediment volume ÷ original suspension volume); F close to 1 is desirable.
- **Degree of flocculation β = F/F∞** (sediment volume of flocculated ÷ deflocculated suspension).
- Redispersibility (number of inversions to resuspend), rheology (viscosity with a Brookfield viscometer), particle size and zeta potential, pH, density, drug content uniformity, microbial limits.

## 2.11 Emulsions

An **emulsion** is a dispersion of one liquid in another immiscible liquid as droplets, stabilised by an emulsifying agent. Oil-in-water (o/w) for oral use (masks oily taste, improves absorption); water-in-oil (w/o) for many topical creams.

**Emulsifying agents:** natural (acacia, tragacanth, gelatin, lecithin, wool fat), surfactants chosen by HLB (sorbitan esters for w/o, polysorbates for o/w; HLB about 3–6 for w/o and 8–18 for o/w), finely divided solids (bentonite, aluminium hydroxide).

**Methods of preparation:** dry gum (continental) method — oil : water : gum = 4 : 2 : 1 for fixed oils, triturating oil with gum then adding water at once to form the primary emulsion; wet gum (English) method — gum mucilage first, oil added slowly; bottle method for volatile oils; in industry, mixers, homogenisers and colloid mills.

**Instability:** creaming (reversible), coalescence and cracking (irreversible), phase inversion, microbial growth, rancidity of oil.

**Tests for type:** dilution test, dye test (water-soluble dye colours the continuous phase of an o/w emulsion), conductivity (o/w conducts), fluorescence.

**Evaluation:** globule size distribution (microscopy), creaming rate, viscosity, phase separation after centrifuging or freeze–thaw cycles, pH, drug content, microbial limits.

## 2.12 Manufacturing considerations, filling and packaging of liquid orals

**Manufacturing considerations:** water quality (purified water), order of mixing, temperature, complete solution or uniform dispersion, avoidance of air entrapment, preservative efficacy, clarity (filtration for solutions), batch homogeneity, cleaning and microbial control of tanks and pipes.

**Equipment:** stainless steel jacketed tanks with stirrers, propeller and turbine mixers, colloid mills and homogenisers, filter presses and cartridge filters, transfer pumps.

**Filling methods:**

| Method | Principle | Suits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gravity filling | Liquid flows from an overhead tank until a level is reached | Thin, free-flowing liquids |
| Vacuum filling | Container under vacuum draws liquid to a level | Thin liquids, glass bottles |
| Piston (volumetric) filling | Piston draws and pushes a fixed volume | Viscous syrups, suspensions, emulsions; accurate volume |
| Pressure / pump filling | Liquid pumped into container | High-speed lines |

**Packaging:** amber glass or plastic (PET, HDPE) bottles; closures such as screw caps with liners, roll-on pilfer-proof (ROPP) aluminium caps, child-resistant caps; measuring cups or droppers; labels and cartons.

**Evaluation of liquid orals (as in the pharmacopoeia):** appearance and clarity, pH, specific gravity or weight per ml, viscosity, drug content (assay), fill volume (extractable volume), alcohol content for elixirs, preservative content, sedimentation and redispersibility (suspensions), globule size (emulsions), microbial limits and freedom from specified organisms, and stability.

## Remember

- Three granulation routes: wet (most common), dry (slugging, roller compaction; for moisture-sensitive drugs), direct compression.
- Capping and lamination come from trapped air, fines and wrong moisture; picking and sticking from moisture and too little lubricant.
- Sugar coating steps: seal → subcoat → smooth → colour → polish → print. Film coat = polymer + plasticiser + solvent + colour.
- Enteric polymers: CAP, HPMCP, Eudragit L/S, shellac.
- IP weight variation (20 tablets): 10% (≤80 mg), 7.5% (80–250 mg), 5% (≥250 mg). Friability ≤1% at 100 revolutions. Disintegration: uncoated 15 min, film 30 min, sugar 60 min, dispersible 3 min, effervescent 5 min, enteric 2 h acid then buffer.
- Simple Syrup IP ≈ 66.7% w/w sucrose; elixir = sweet hydroalcoholic solution.
- Stokes' law v = d²(ρs − ρl)g/18η; F = Vu/Vo; flocculated suspensions do not cake.
- Dry gum ratio 4 : 2 : 1 (oil : water : gum) for fixed oils.

# Unit 3: Capsules and pellets

Capsules hold a drug inside a soluble shell made mainly of gelatin. They come in two kinds: **hard gelatin capsules**, filled with powders, granules or pellets, and **soft gelatin capsules**, filled mostly with liquids or pastes and sealed in one piece. This unit also covers **pellets**, small free-flowing spheres often filled into hard capsules.

## 3.1 Capsules: introduction

A **capsule** is a solid dosage form in which the drug, with or without excipients, is enclosed in a hard or soft soluble shell.

**Advantages:** tasteless and odourless to swallow; easy to fill in small or large batches; fewer excipients and less pressure than tablets, so good for drugs that compress poorly; quick release (shell dissolves in a few minutes); attractive colours for identification; can hold powders, pellets, tablets, semisolids or liquids; soft capsules give accurate liquid doses and better bioavailability for oily, poorly soluble drugs.

**Disadvantages:** not for very soluble salts that irritate the stomach (high local concentration, e.g. potassium chloride, bromides); not for highly efflorescent or deliquescent materials (they soften or dry out the shell); not suited to children who cannot swallow; gelatin is of animal origin (some patients refuse it); shells are sensitive to humidity and heat.

**Gelatin:** obtained by partial hydrolysis of collagen from animal skin, bones and connective tissue.

| Type | Process | Source | Isoelectric point (approx.) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Type A | Acid treatment | Mainly pork skin | pH 7–9 |
| Type B | Alkali (lime) treatment | Bones and cattle hides | pH 4.7–5 |

Mixtures of A and B are used to balance clarity, strength and plasticity. Gel strength is measured as **Bloom strength** (grams of force needed to depress a standard plunger into a set gel); capsule gelatin has a fairly high Bloom value. Viscosity controls the shell thickness.

**Non-gelatin shells:** hydroxypropyl methylcellulose (HPMC) and pullulan capsules are used for vegetarian products and moisture-sensitive drugs, because they hold less water.

## 3.2 Hard gelatin capsules

### a. Production of hard gelatin capsule shells

Shells are made in two pieces, a **body** and a slightly wider **cap**, by **dip moulding** on automatic machines.

```text
1 Dipping        stainless steel pins (moulds), lubricated, dipped in a warm gelatin solution
2 Spinning       pins rotated so the film spreads evenly
3 Drying         cool, controlled-humidity air sets and dries the film
4 Stripping      dried shells pulled off the pins
5 Trimming       cut to exact length
6 Joining        caps and bodies pre-locked together
7 Printing       identification ink (optional)
8 Sorting/packing in moisture-proof cartons
```

**Shell composition:** gelatin; colourants (dyes, iron oxides); opacifier (titanium dioxide); preservatives; sometimes a surfactant for wetting the pins; water. Hard shells contain about 13–16% moisture. Below this range they become brittle; above it they soften and stick.

**Locking designs:** traditional plain shells, and self-locking shells (Coni-Snap, Lok-Cap and similar) with grooves or dimples that hold the cap firmly and prevent separation on high-speed machines. Tapered body rims help the cap fit without splitting.

### b. Size of capsules

Sizes are numbered from 000 (largest) to 5 (smallest).

| Size | 000 | 00 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Approx. volume (ml) | 1.37 | 0.95 | 0.68 | 0.50 | 0.37 | 0.30 | 0.21 | 0.13 |

Size 000 is rarely used for humans because it is hard to swallow; sizes 0 to 4 are common. Larger sizes (e.g. 10, 11, 12) are for veterinary use.

**Choosing the size:** the fill weight is decided by the dose and the bulk (tapped) density of the powder. Fill volume needed = fill weight ÷ tapped density. Example: 300 mg of a blend of tapped density 0.6 g/ml needs 0.5 ml → size 1 capsule. If the volume is not filled, diluent is added; the smallest size that holds the dose is chosen.

### c. Filling of hard gelatin capsules

**Formulation of the fill:** drug + diluent (lactose, microcrystalline cellulose, starch) + glidant (colloidal silica) + lubricant (magnesium stearate) + disintegrant/wetting agent where needed (sodium lauryl sulphate helps hydrophobic drugs). The powder must flow well and, for dosator and tamping machines, form a loose plug.

**Steps:** rectification (orientation of empty capsules, body down) → separation of cap from body → filling of the body → joining (closing) the cap → ejection.

| Method | How it works |
| --- | --- |
| Hand filling | Powder spread on a tile and capsules punched into it; for small extemporaneous lots |
| Hand-operated filling machine (e.g. Feton type) | Plate with 100 to 300 holes; bodies in holes, powder spread and levelled, caps replaced |
| Auger (screw) fill | Rotating auger pushes powder into bodies; older semi-automatic machines |
| Vibratory fill | Vibration settles powder into bodies |
| Dosator (piston-tamp, e.g. Zanasi type) | Hollow tube dips into powder bed, piston forms a plug, ejects it into the body |
| Dosing disc (tamping, e.g. Bosch/Höfliger type) | Powder tamped several times into holes of a disc to form plugs, then pushed into bodies |

Pellets, granules, tablets and semisolid or liquid fills (with band sealing) can also be filled into hard shells.

### d. Finishing

After filling, capsules are cleaned and polished to remove adhering powder: by tumbling with sodium chloride crystals, by cloth-lined pans, by brushes, or by automatic de-dusting and polishing machines. Sealing or banding (a strip of gelatin around the joint) prevents tampering and leakage of liquid fills.

### e. Special techniques of formulation

- **Enteric or modified-release capsules:** coating the filled capsule, filling enteric-coated pellets, or using acid-resistant shells.
- **Sustained release:** filling a mix of pellets with different coatings.
- **Liquid and semisolid fills:** thermosoftening or thixotropic fills filled hot and sealed by banding.
- **Combination fills:** tablet + powder, pellets + tablet, for incompatible drugs kept apart.
- **Taste and odour masking** of drugs such as fish oils, and protection of light-sensitive drugs by opaque shells.

### f. Manufacturing defects of hard capsules

Splitting of caps or bodies, telescoping (cap pushed down over the body too far), dented or crushed shells, double caps, uneven or short fill (weight variation), powder on the outside, broken or loose caps, holes or cracks, bubbles, colour or printing faults, brittleness (too dry) or softness and sticking (too humid).

### g. In-process and final product quality control tests

**In process:** fill weight checks at intervals, appearance, locking, moisture of shells and powder, flow of the blend.

**Finished product:**

1. **Appearance:** uniform size, colour, shape, no defects, clean printing.
2. **Uniformity of weight (IP):** weigh 20 intact capsules individually, then empty each and weigh the shells to get the content weight. Not more than two may differ from the average content weight by more than the percentage below, and none by more than twice that percentage.

| Average content weight | Allowed deviation |
| --- | --- |
| Less than 300 mg | 10% |
| 300 mg or more | 7.5% |

3. **Disintegration test:** IP apparatus as for tablets with discs; hard gelatin capsules usually must disintegrate within 30 minutes unless the monograph says otherwise; enteric capsules are tested first in acid, then in buffer.
4. **Dissolution test:** basket or paddle (with a sinker so capsules do not float).
5. **Uniformity of content** for low-dose capsules.
6. **Assay**, moisture content and microbial limits where required.

## 3.3 Soft gelatin capsules

**Soft gelatin capsules (softgels)** are one-piece, hermetically sealed shells made of gelatin with a plasticiser, filled usually with liquids, solutions, suspensions or pastes. They may be round, oval, oblong or tube-shaped.

**Uses:** oily vitamins (A, D, E), fish oils, cardiac glycosides and other potent drugs needing exact doses, poorly soluble drugs dissolved in oils or polyethylene glycols (better absorption), cyclosporin-type lipid systems, nifedipine, paracetamol liquid-fill, chewable and bath capsules, suppository and vaginal capsules.

### a. Nature of the shell

| Component | Role | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gelatin | Film former | Type A/B blends |
| Plasticiser | Makes the shell elastic | Glycerin, sorbitol, propylene glycol |
| Water | Solvent; much removed during drying | Purified water |
| Others | Appearance, protection | Colours, opacifier (titanium dioxide), preservatives, flavours |

The ratio of dry plasticiser to dry gelatin decides how soft or hard the shell is; ratios of roughly 0.4 to 1.0 cover shells from relatively hard to very soft. The finished shell keeps some water (about 6–10%).

### b. Nature of the capsule content

The fill must not dissolve, soften or harden the shell. Suitable: vegetable and mineral oils, medium-chain triglycerides, PEG 400 and 600, non-ionic surfactants, suspensions of solids in these. Unsuitable: water above about 5%, low-molecular-weight water-soluble solvents (ethanol, small alcohols) in large amounts, aldehydes (cross-link gelatin), emulsions (water migrates), strongly acidic (below about pH 2.5) or alkaline (above about pH 7.5) fills.

### c. Size of soft capsules

Soft capsules are described by shape and by the volume they hold, expressed in **minims** (1 minim ≈ 0.0616 ml), for example "10 oblong" or "5 round", rather than by the 000–5 numbers used for hard shells.

### d. Base adsorption and minim/gram factor

When a solid drug is suspended in a liquid base for filling, two factors help calculate the fill:

- **Base adsorption (BA):** grams of liquid base needed to wet and make 1 g of solid into a fillable, flowing paste. BA = weight of base ÷ weight of solid.
- **Minim/gram factor (M/g):** the volume in minims occupied by 1 g of solid plus the base needed to suspend it (its base adsorption). It is found by measuring the volume of the mixture. Fill volume per capsule = M/g × weight of solid per capsule.

**Worked example (illustrative figures):** a solid has BA = 0.7, so each gram of solid needs 0.7 g of base. If the mixture of 1 g solid + 0.7 g base occupies 25 minims, M/g = 25. A dose of 0.4 g of solid per capsule needs 0.4 × 25 = 10 minims of fill, so a capsule holding about 10 minims is chosen. Lower base adsorption gives a smaller capsule, so solids of fine, regular particles are preferred.

### e. Production of soft capsules

| Method | Principle |
| --- | --- |
| Plate process | Warm gelatin sheet laid over a die plate, fill poured in, second sheet placed on top, upper plate pressed to seal and cut; batch method, now largely historical |
| Rotary die process (Scherer) | Two gelatin ribbons pass between two rotating dies; fill injected between ribbons through a wedge just as the dies seal and cut the capsule; continuous, accurate, most widely used |
| Reciprocating die (Norton) | Ribbons pass between vertical dies that open and close; similar to rotary |
| Accogel process | Rotary process that can fill dry powders into soft shells |
| Seamless (bubble) method | Concentric nozzle drops gelatin and fill together into cold oil; makes seamless spheres |

After forming, capsules are washed to remove lubricant oil, tumble-dried and then tray-dried in low-humidity tunnels to the right moisture and hardness.

### f. In-process and final quality control tests (soft capsules)

In process: ribbon thickness, seal thickness and strength, fill weight, shell weight, shell moisture, hardness after drying. Final: appearance and leaks, uniformity of weight, uniformity of content, disintegration and dissolution, assay, moisture, microbial limits, burst strength / seal integrity, freedom from leaks after storage.

### g. Packing, storage and stability testing

- **Packing:** blister packs (PVC/PVDC with aluminium foil), strips, glass or HDPE bottles with desiccant where needed.
- **Storage:** cool, dry place away from heat and high humidity; high humidity makes shells soft and sticky, heat can melt or deform them, and very low humidity makes them brittle.
- **Stability testing:** shell–fill interaction (migration of fill components into the shell, cross-linking of gelatin by aldehydes that slows dissolution), physical changes (hardening, softening, leakage, colour), chemical assay over time under long-term and accelerated conditions, and dissolution changes. Cross-linking shows as a skin (pellicle) that slows dissolution; enzymes (pepsin or pancreatin) in the medium may be allowed to digest it in dissolution testing.

### h. Applications of soft capsules

Oral (liquids, oils, vitamins, potent drugs), chewable softgels, vaginal and rectal capsules, topical "twist-off" single-dose capsules, bath and cosmetic capsules, and better bioavailability for poorly water-soluble drugs presented in solution.

## 3.4 Pellets

**Pellets** are small, free-flowing, near-spherical agglomerates of drug and excipients, usually 0.5 to 1.5 mm in size, made for oral modified-release or multiparticulate systems. They are filled into hard capsules or compressed into tablets.

### a. Advantages of pellets

1. Spread evenly through the gut, so absorption is more uniform and less affected by stomach emptying.
2. Less risk of dose dumping than a single-unit sustained-release tablet.
3. Lower risk of local irritation.
4. Good flow and packing, uniform fill weights.
5. Pellets of different drugs or release rates can be mixed in one capsule.
6. Smooth surface suits even coating.

### b. Formulation requirements

| Component | Purpose | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drug | Active | — |
| Spheronisation aid / filler | Plasticity and water holding for extrusion and rounding | Microcrystalline cellulose (most important), lactose, mannitol |
| Binder | Strength | Povidone, HPMC |
| Granulating liquid | Wets mass | Water, water–alcohol |
| Others | Release control, disintegration, stability | Polymers, surfactants, buffers |
| Starter cores (layering) | Base to build on | Sugar spheres (non-pareils), MCC spheres |

Ideal pellets are spherical, of narrow size range, with a smooth surface, good strength and low friability, and good flow.

### c. Pelletisation processes

1. **Extrusion–spheronisation (most common):**

```text
Dry mixing → wet massing (granulating liquid) → extrusion through a screen (cylindrical extrudates)
   → spheronisation (extrudates broken and rolled into spheres on a rotating friction plate)
   → drying → sieving/size classification → coating (optional)
```

2. **Powder layering:** dry drug powder sprinkled onto starter cores wetted with binder solution in a coating pan or rotor.
3. **Solution or suspension layering:** drug solution or suspension sprayed onto inert cores in a fluidised bed (Wurster) or pan.
4. **Spray drying and spray congealing:** droplets dried by hot air (spray drying) or solidified by cooling of a melt (spray congealing) to give small spheres.
5. **Balling (spherical agglomeration):** powder wetted and tumbled in a drum or pan so particles roll into spheres.
6. **Cryopelletisation:** drops of liquid formulation frozen in liquid nitrogen, then freeze-dried.
7. **Melt pelletisation / hot-melt extrusion** with molten binders.
8. **Compression** into mini-tablets (a related approach).

### d. Equipment for manufacture of pellets

- **Extruders:** screw (axial or radial), sieve and basket, roll and ram extruders.
- **Spheroniser (marumeriser):** a bowl with a fast-rotating grooved friction plate at the bottom.
- **Fluidised bed with Wurster insert** or rotor (tangential spray) for layering and coating.
- **Coating pans** for powder layering.
- **Centrifugal (rotary) granulators** (e.g. CF granulator) that combine layering and rounding.
- **Spray dryers and spray congealers.**
- **Fluid-bed or tray dryers** and vibratory sieves for sizing.

**Evaluation of pellets:** size distribution (sieve analysis), shape (sphericity, aspect ratio by image analysis), surface (microscopy), density, flow, friability and crushing strength, drug content, dissolution and release profile.

## Remember

- Gelatin Type A (acid, pork skin, IEP 7–9); Type B (alkali, bones/hides, IEP 4.7–5). Bloom strength = gel strength.
- Hard shells: dip moulding (dip → spin → dry → strip → trim → join); 13–16% moisture.
- Capsule sizes 000 (1.37 ml) to 5 (0.13 ml); choose by fill weight ÷ tapped density.
- Filling machines: hand plate, auger, dosator (Zanasi), dosing disc (Bosch/Höfliger).
- IP weight variation of capsules (20): less than 300 mg → 10%; 300 mg or more → 7.5%.
- Soft capsules: gelatin + plasticiser (glycerin/sorbitol) + water; rotary die process; base adsorption = g base/g solid; minim/gram factor = minims per g of solid in its base.
- Unsuitable softgel fills: much water, aldehydes, emulsions, strongly acidic or alkaline fills.
- Pellets 0.5–1.5 mm; extrusion–spheronisation with microcrystalline cellulose; also layering, spray drying/congealing, cryopelletisation.

# Unit 4: Parenteral products and ophthalmic preparations

Parenteral and ophthalmic products go straight into the body or onto the delicate eye, bypassing the body's normal defences. They must therefore be **sterile**, and injections must also be **free from pyrogens and visible particles**. This unit explains how such products are formulated, made, filled and tested.

## Part A: Parenteral products

## 4.1 Definition, types, advantages and limitations

**Parenteral preparations** are sterile preparations intended for administration by injection, infusion or implantation into the body, avoiding the gastrointestinal tract (Greek *para enteron*, "beside the intestine").

**Types (by form)**

| Type | Description | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Solutions (injections) | Drug dissolved in a vehicle | Calcium gluconate injection |
| Suspensions | Insoluble drug dispersed; not for IV | Procaine penicillin, some depot steroids |
| Emulsions | Oil-in-water for IV nutrition or drug delivery | Fat emulsion, propofol |
| Sterile powders for reconstitution | Dry powder dissolved before use | Ampicillin, ceftriaxone |
| Large-volume parenterals (infusions) | 100 ml or more, single-dose, usually IV | Dextrose, sodium chloride, Ringer lactate |
| Small-volume parenterals | Less than 100 ml | Ampoules, vials |
| Implants | Solid pellets placed under the skin | Hormone implants |

**Types (by route):** intravenous, intramuscular, subcutaneous, intradermal, and specialised routes (intra-arterial, intrathecal, intra-articular, intracardiac, epidural).

**Advantages:** rapid action (emergencies); 100% bioavailability by IV; useful when the patient cannot take oral medicine (unconscious, vomiting); for drugs destroyed or not absorbed orally (insulin, heparin); controlled and depot effects; correction of fluid and electrolyte balance; total parenteral nutrition.

**Limitations:** pain and fear; needs trained staff; once given, hard to reverse; risk of infection, thrombophlebitis, embolism and tissue damage; expensive to make (sterility, clean rooms, pyrogen control); strict quality standards.

## 4.2 Preformulation factors and essential requirements

**Preformulation factors:** solubility in water and at physiological pH; pKa and the risk of precipitation on dilution in blood; stability in solution (hydrolysis, oxidation) and to heat (decides the sterilisation method); light sensitivity; compatibility with containers, closures and infusion fluids; particle size (for suspensions); polymorphic form.

**Essential requirements of parenterals:**

1. Sterility — free from living micro-organisms.
2. Freedom from pyrogens (bacterial endotoxins).
3. Freedom from visible and limited sub-visible particles.
4. Stability — chemical, physical and microbiological.
5. Isotonicity with body fluids (as far as possible), and a pH close to 7.4 where stability allows.
6. Correct and uniform content and volume.
7. Compatibility with containers and closures.

## 4.3 Vehicles

| Vehicle | Points |
| --- | --- |
| Water for Injections (WFI) | Main vehicle; prepared by distillation (multiple-effect stills) or an equally effective validated process; must be pyrogen-free; stored hot (about 80 °C) and circulated to prevent growth |
| Sterile Water for Injections | WFI sterilised in single-dose containers for dissolving powders |
| Bacteriostatic water | Contains a preservative; not for neonates or large volumes |
| Water-miscible cosolvents | Ethanol, propylene glycol, polyethylene glycol, glycerin — for poorly water-soluble drugs (diazepam, phenytoin, digoxin) |
| Non-aqueous (oily) vehicles | Fixed oils such as sesame, arachis, cottonseed, ethyl oleate; for IM depot injections only (testosterone, progesterone esters); must be free of mineral oil, rancidity and moisture |

## 4.4 Additives (excipients) in parenterals

| Additive | Purpose | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Antimicrobial preservatives | Multi-dose containers; not used in large-volume infusions or intrathecal/intracardiac injections | Benzyl alcohol, phenol, cresol, chlorocresol, methyl and propyl paraben, benzalkonium chloride, thiomersal |
| Antioxidants | Prevent oxidation | Sodium metabisulphite, sodium bisulphite, ascorbic acid, BHA, BHT, tocopherols |
| Chelating agents | Bind metal ions that catalyse oxidation | Disodium edetate |
| Buffers | Hold pH for stability and comfort | Acetate, citrate, phosphate |
| Tonicity agents | Make isotonic | Sodium chloride, dextrose, glycerin |
| Solubilisers / surfactants | Increase solubility, wet particles | Polysorbate 80, lecithin, cyclodextrins |
| Suspending agents | Suspensions | Sodium CMC, methylcellulose |
| Bulking agents | Lyophilised cakes | Mannitol, lactose, glycine |
| Local anaesthetic | Reduce pain | Benzyl alcohol, lignocaine |
| Inert gases | Displace oxygen | Nitrogen, carbon dioxide |

## 4.5 Importance of isotonicity

A solution is **isotonic** when it has the same osmotic pressure as body fluids (blood, tears), so cells neither swell nor shrink. **0.9% w/v sodium chloride** is isotonic with blood; blood and tears freeze at about −0.52 °C.

- **Hypotonic** solutions make red cells swell and burst (haemolysis).
- **Hypertonic** solutions make cells shrink (crenation) and cause pain and tissue irritation.
- Isotonicity matters most for IV infusions, subcutaneous and intrathecal injections and eye preparations. Hypertonic IV solutions can be given slowly into large veins (e.g. total parenteral nutrition through central lines).

**Adjusting tonicity — freezing-point method:** W = (0.52 − a)/b, where W is g of adjusting substance per 100 ml, a is the freezing-point depression of the unadjusted solution and b is the depression caused by 1% w/v of the adjusting substance (0.576 °C for NaCl).

**Worked example:** a 1% w/v solution of a drug has a freezing-point depression of 0.10 °C. W = (0.52 − 0.10)/0.576 = 0.73 g NaCl per 100 ml.

Other methods: sodium chloride equivalent (E) method and the White–Vincent method (V = w × E × 111.1).

## 4.6 Production procedure

```text
Cleaning of containers & closures → washing, rinsing with WFI → depyrogenation of glass (dry heat)
                                             ↓
Compounding: weigh, dissolve in WFI, add additives, adjust pH and volume (in clean area)
                                             ↓
Filtration: clarifying filtration, then sterilising filtration (0.22 µm) where used
                                             ↓
Filling into ampoules/vials/bags in an aseptic area → sealing (ampoules) or stoppering and capping (vials)
                                             ↓
Terminal sterilisation (autoclave, e.g. 121 °C for 15 minutes) if the product can stand heat
                                             ↓
Quality control tests → inspection for particles and leaks → labelling and packing → release
```

**Sterilisation methods:**

| Method | Conditions (typical) | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Moist heat (autoclave) | 121 °C for 15 minutes (or validated equivalents) | Aqueous solutions in sealed containers, rubber closures, garments |
| Dry heat (hot-air oven/tunnel) | 160 °C for 2 hours or equivalent; higher temperatures (about 250 °C) for depyrogenation | Glassware, metal items, oils, powders |
| Filtration | 0.22 µm membrane | Heat-sensitive solutions |
| Ionising radiation | Gamma rays, electron beam | Disposables, some powders |
| Gas (ethylene oxide) | Controlled humidity and temperature | Plastic devices, not solutions |

**Removal of pyrogens:** pyrogens (mainly bacterial endotoxins, lipopolysaccharides from Gram-negative bacteria) are heat-stable and pass through ordinary filters. They are prevented by using WFI, clean materials and good hygiene, and removed from glassware by dry heat at high temperature (about 250 °C) or chemical treatment.

## 4.7 Production facilities and controls

**Layout of a parenteral unit (areas of increasing cleanliness):**

```text
Clean-up area (washing) → Compounding area → Aseptic filling area (core, cleanest)
       ↑ material airlocks, pass boxes, personnel change rooms ↑
Quarantine & packaging areas outside
```

**Clean room grades (EU/WHO GMP, used in Schedule M):**

| Grade | Use | Equivalent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Aseptic filling zone, open containers (laminar airflow) | ISO 5 (old class 100) |
| B | Background to Grade A | ISO 5 at rest, ISO 7 in operation |
| C | Less critical steps, e.g. preparation of solutions to be filtered | ISO 7 at rest |
| D | Handling components after washing | ISO 8 at rest |

**Environmental controls:** HEPA-filtered air (removes at least 99.97% of 0.3 µm particles); laminar (unidirectional) airflow over critical zones; positive pressure cascades from clean to less clean rooms; control of temperature and humidity; smooth, non-shedding, easily cleaned walls, floors and ceilings with coved corners; no sinks or drains in aseptic areas; monitoring of air particles, settle plates, contact plates and surfaces.

**Personnel:** trained, healthy staff; sterile gowns, hoods, masks, gloves and boots; gowning procedures; minimum number of people and movements in aseptic rooms.

## 4.8 Aseptic processing

**Aseptic processing** is filling a product that has been sterilised (by filtration or other methods) into sterile containers, and sealing them, in an environment that prevents microbial contamination. Used when the product cannot be terminally sterilised (proteins, many antibiotics, lyophilised products).

Key points: sterile components (containers, stoppers, equipment), sterile filtration of solutions, Grade A filling under laminar airflow with Grade B background, isolators and restricted access barrier systems, blow–fill–seal machines, and **media fill (process simulation)** runs with growth medium in place of product to prove the process keeps out contamination.

## 4.9 Formulation of injections, sterile powders, LVPs and lyophilised products

**Injections (solutions):** drug + WFI + buffer + tonicity agent ± antioxidant, chelating agent and preservative; pH chosen for stability and comfort; filled under nitrogen if oxidisable. Example: ascorbic acid injection — ascorbic acid neutralised partly with sodium bicarbonate, edetate disodium, filled under nitrogen.

**Sterile powders:** for drugs unstable in solution (many penicillins and cephalosporins). Made by (i) sterile crystallisation and aseptic powder filling into vials, (ii) spray drying, or (iii) freeze drying. Reconstituted with sterile water before use. Need good flow for accurate powder filling and low moisture.

**Large-volume parenterals (LVPs):** 100 ml or more, single-dose, given by IV infusion; must be sterile, pyrogen-free, free of particles and, as far as possible, isotonic; must **not contain antimicrobial preservatives**; terminally sterilised. Examples: dextrose 5%, sodium chloride 0.9%, Ringer's and Ringer lactate, amino acids, mannitol, fat emulsions, plasma expanders (dextran). Containers: glass bottles, PVC or non-PVC plastic bags, blow–fill–seal bottles.

**Lyophilised (freeze-dried) products:** water is removed from a frozen product by sublimation under vacuum, giving a dry cake that dissolves quickly.

```text
Freezing (below the eutectic or collapse temperature)
   → Primary drying (ice sublimes under vacuum; shelf heated gently)
   → Secondary drying (bound water removed by desorption at higher shelf temperature)
   → Stoppering under vacuum or nitrogen inside the chamber → capping
```

Uses: proteins, vaccines, some antibiotics, heat- and moisture-sensitive drugs. Formulation includes bulking agents (mannitol, glycine), cryoprotectants and lyoprotectants (sucrose, trehalose) and buffers. Advantages: long shelf life, quick reconstitution, no heat. Disadvantages: costly equipment, long cycle, risk of collapse or melt-back.

## 4.10 Containers and closures

**Glass** (IP types):

| Type | Composition | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type I | Borosilicate glass; high hydrolytic resistance | Most parenterals, including alkaline and unbuffered products |
| Type II | Soda-lime glass with surface treatment (de-alkalised) | Acidic and neutral aqueous products, many infusion bottles |
| Type III | Soda-lime glass, untreated | Non-aqueous injections and dry powders (if suitable) |

**Plastics:** polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC and non-PVC bags for infusions; advantages of light weight and no breakage; concerns of leaching (plasticiser such as DEHP), permeation and sorption of drugs (e.g. glyceryl trinitrate, diazepam to PVC).

**Rubber closures:** natural, butyl, chlorobutyl, bromobutyl and silicone rubbers. Butyl-type rubbers have low gas and moisture permeability and are preferred. Problems: leaching of additives, sorption of preservatives, coring (pieces cut by the needle), fragmentation. Closures are washed, siliconised, sterilised and often coated (e.g. with fluoropolymer).

**Selection of containers and closures** depends on chemical compatibility, protection from light and moisture, single- or multi-dose use, sterilisation method, and convenience.

## 4.11 Filling and sealing of ampoules, vials and infusion fluids

- **Ampoules:** filled with a needle reaching below the neck to avoid wetting it; nitrogen flushing if required. **Sealing:** tip sealing (melting the tip — may leave a weak bead) or **pull sealing** (heating the neck while rotating and pulling the top off; gives a more reliable seal). Ampoule sealing machines combine filling and sealing.
- **Vials:** filled by volumetric piston or peristaltic pumps; rubber stopper inserted; aluminium seal crimped on (flip-off caps).
- **Infusion fluids:** bottles or bags filled by volumetric or gravity fillers in clean areas, stoppered and capped or heat-sealed; blow–fill–seal makes, fills and seals plastic containers in one step.
- **Overfill:** a small excess volume is added so that the labelled volume can be withdrawn (extractable volume).

## 4.12 Quality control tests of parenteral products

| Test | Outline |
| --- | --- |
| Sterility test (IP) | Membrane filtration (preferred) or direct inoculation into fluid thioglycollate medium (incubated at 30–35 °C, mainly for anaerobes and bacteria) and soybean–casein digest medium (20–25 °C, fungi and aerobes); incubate 14 days; no growth = passes |
| Bacterial endotoxin test (BET) | Limulus amoebocyte lysate (LAL) reacts with endotoxin: gel-clot, turbidimetric or chromogenic methods |
| Pyrogen test (rabbit test) | Product injected into the ear vein of healthy rabbits; rectal temperature recorded for 3 hours; rise compared with pharmacopoeial limits |
| Particulate matter | Visible: inspection against black and white backgrounds under good light. Sub-visible: light obscuration or microscopy. For LVPs the usual limits are not more than 25 particles per ml of 10 µm or larger and not more than 3 per ml of 25 µm or larger; for SVPs, not more than 6000 per container of 10 µm or larger and 600 of 25 µm or larger |
| Leaker test (ampoules) | Ampoules immersed in coloured dye (methylene blue) under vacuum; leaking ampoules take up dye. Vials are tested by other integrity tests |
| Others | Extractable volume, pH, assay, clarity, uniformity of content/weight (powders), osmolality, bacterial endotoxins limit, container closure integrity |

## Part B: Ophthalmic preparations

## 4.13 Introduction and formulation considerations

**Ophthalmic preparations** are sterile products applied to the eye surface or into the eye: eye drops (solutions and suspensions), eye ointments, eye lotions, gels, inserts and intraocular injections.

The eye has little defence: tears drain quickly through the nasolacrimal duct, so only a small part of a drop stays in contact. An infected eye (e.g. *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* contamination) can lose sight quickly, so sterility is essential.

**Formulation considerations**

1. **Sterility and preservation:** sterile; multi-dose containers need a preservative — benzalkonium chloride (often around 0.01%), chlorobutanol, phenylmercuric nitrate or acetate, thiomersal, chlorhexidine; often with disodium edetate to improve activity against *Pseudomonas*.
2. **Tonicity:** close to tears (0.9% NaCl equivalent); the eye tolerates a fairly wide range without much discomfort.
3. **pH and buffering:** tears are near pH 7.4; a pH close to this is most comfortable, but some drugs need a lower pH for stability (pilocarpine, adrenaline); low buffer capacity lets tears bring the pH back quickly.
4. **Viscosity:** increasing viscosity (methylcellulose, HPMC, polyvinyl alcohol, carbomer) prolongs contact time.
5. **Clarity:** solutions free from particles (filtration).
6. **Stability:** antioxidants (sodium metabisulphite) for oxidisable drugs.
7. **Particle size:** suspensions and ointments must contain very fine particles to avoid irritation.
8. **Packaging:** sterile, tamper-evident containers.

## 4.14 Formulation of eye drops, eye ointments and eye lotions

| Preparation | Typical composition |
| --- | --- |
| Eye drops (solution) | Drug, buffer, tonicity agent, preservative, viscosity agent, antioxidant, purified water (sterile); e.g. chloramphenicol, timolol, pilocarpine eye drops |
| Eye drops (suspension) | Very fine drug, suspending agent, wetting agent, preservative; e.g. prednisolone acetate |
| Eye ointment | Drug in a sterile, non-irritant base, commonly yellow or white soft paraffin with liquid paraffin and wool fat (wool fat helps take up water); e.g. chloramphenicol, tetracycline eye ointments |
| Eye lotion | Large-volume sterile isotonic solution for washing the eye (first aid), e.g. sodium chloride eye lotion; usually without preservative, single-use |

## 4.15 Methods of preparation

- **Eye drops:** dissolve ingredients in water → filter to clarify → sterilise by (a) heating in the final sealed container (autoclave) if stable, or (b) sterile filtration (0.22 µm) and aseptic filling into sterile containers.
- **Eye ointments:** base melted, filtered hot and sterilised by dry heat (paraffins withstand dry heat); drug finely powdered and sterilised separately or dissolved; incorporated aseptically; filled into sterile collapsible tubes.
- **Eye lotions:** prepared like solutions and sterilised by autoclaving in their final containers.

## 4.16 Labelling and containers

**Containers:** glass or plastic dropper bottles; plastic squeeze bottles (LDPE) with dropper tips; single-dose units (blow–fill–seal); small collapsible metal or plastic tubes with narrow nozzles for ointments; tamper-evident seals. Containers protect from light and contamination and must not react with the product.

**Labelling:** name and strength of drug, preservative, "sterile", "not to be used more than 4 weeks after first opening" or the stated period, storage conditions, batch number, expiry date, "for external use only" where relevant, and directions. Eye lotions: "not for injection" and "use once and discard".

## 4.17 Evaluation of ophthalmic preparations

1. Sterility test.
2. Clarity and particle examination for solutions; particle size for suspensions and ointments.
3. pH and tonicity (osmolality).
4. Viscosity.
5. Drug content (assay) and preservative content.
6. Preservative efficacy (antimicrobial effectiveness) test.
7. For eye ointments: metal particles test (IP) and leakage test of tubes.
8. Container–closure integrity and stability studies; irritation tests on development products.

## Remember

- Parenteral essentials: sterile, pyrogen-free, particle-free, stable, isotonic where possible.
- WFI by distillation; stored hot and circulated. Oily vehicles only for IM.
- No preservatives in LVPs or intrathecal/intracardiac injections.
- Isotonic = 0.9% NaCl; freezing point −0.52 °C; W = (0.52 − a)/b with b = 0.576 for NaCl.
- Autoclave 121 °C 15 min; dry heat 160 °C 2 h; depyrogenation at about 250 °C; filtration 0.22 µm.
- Grade A = ISO 5 under laminar airflow; HEPA ≥ 99.97% at 0.3 µm.
- Lyophilisation: freezing → primary drying (sublimation) → secondary drying (desorption).
- Glass: Type I borosilicate, Type II treated soda-lime, Type III soda-lime.
- Sterility test: thioglycollate (30–35 °C) + soybean–casein digest (20–25 °C), 14 days; BET by LAL; leaker test with methylene blue.
- Eye preparations: sterile; benzalkonium chloride + edetate; viscosity agents prolong contact; eye ointment base = soft paraffin + liquid paraffin + wool fat.
